subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The house resumed, from Thursday, March 10, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Howe (Port Arthur)-Mr. Robinson (Sirncoe East) in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure respecting the Canada Grain Act to amend the statutory grades of western grain and eastern grain with respect to the grade No. 3 amber Durum wheat and all grades of soybeans as recommended by the committee on western and eastern grain standards: to provide for the appointment of four in lieu of three assistant grain commissioners and to increase the annual salaries of the chief and other two commissioners from fourteen and twelve thousand dollars to fifteen and thirteen thousand five hundred dollars respectively.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext:
In discussing this resolution last evening objection was raised to the way the resolution was introduced. Objection was raised to the fact that it was introduced as a package deal. I know that if I am going to make a purchase of anything I want to be sure that the whole object is sound. If I am going to buy a barrel of apples and find some good apples on top, I am going to look into the bottom of the barrel to see what is there. In this case, the first portion of the resolution appears to be a necessary and timely move, but as we dig down into the barrel we find that the apples are not in particularly good condition.
We questioned the necessity for action at this time to raise the salaries of the members of the board of grain commissioners in the proportion that is envisaged in the resolution. Perhaps the work that the assistant commissioners have to do in the western provinces, if properly carried out, would necessitate the appointment of an additional assistant commissioner. Last night, however, I pointed out the inefficiency of one particular commissioner in investigating a contravention of the Canada Grain Act. I pointed out, too, that although two of the commissioners were aware of the charge they had taken no action. It was not until the matter was aired before the standing committee on agriculture and colonization that these policemen of the Canada Grain Act took action, and eventually did fine the company that was stealing half a cent a bushel from the farmers.
I feel that in any form of business it is necessary to have certain principles to which one must stick in promoting individuals from within the ranks. I have always assumed that the most desirable principle is to promote individuals according to their ability. As a vacancy occurred in the top levels, those who have been working for many years at

a lower level and who are qualified should automatically step up to the senior position. However, the government of today seems to adopt a different principle in making appointments to these lucrative positions. Perhaps ability is not a factor, because if we go over the members of this board of grain commissioners, we find that the chief commissioner, Mr. McKenzie, has an impressive background. He was a Liberal member in the Manitoba legislature and was minister of agriculture in that house from 1932 to 1936. He was also a director of the United Grain Growers.
We find another of the commissioners, Mr. Vallance, was a Liberal member of the House of Commons. The third commissioner, Mr. Milner, did not have the qualification of being a Liberal member in the legislature or the House of Commons. His next best qualification was the fact he had been president of the Winnipeg grain exchange and the manager of a line elevator company. It appears, however, that in recent years the government has become so lavish in their appointments that they diminished the supply. We note that Mr. Frank Chester, whose claim to fame was his defeat by the hon. member for Winnipeg North, was given a position at $10,000 a year on the Canadian farm loan board. Mr. Dewar, who was familiar with this house, was also taken care of, but I imagine the unfortunate good luck at the last election returned a lot of these expectant appointees to the House of Commons instead of the other fields of endeavour.
But the government was not taken aback. They appraised the situation and found that in Saskatchewan the acting house leader of the Liberal party in that province had been doing a good job for the Minister of Agriculture. We noticed his activities during the fall months, and in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of November 6, 1954, we note what Mr. Loptson said:
He told the meeting not to discount the possibility of a "dark horse" entering the contest. I think I am safe in saying you will see Dr. L. B. Thomson (director of P.F.R.A.) in the race.
A man who has been able to pick these winners would deserve a little consideration. I think those of us who are familiar with the political situation in Saskatchewan felt that he had made a good try but he did not win the prize. The Minister of Agriculture had not struck out yet. He looked around and found that the only son of this faithful servant was also a director of the United Grain Growers. Here, we have the same qualification as the two other commissioners, that of being closely attached to the Liberal party and closely attached to the United Grain Growers. The Minister of Agriculture
Canada Grain Act
took a wild swing at the ball, hit a foul ball, but the Minister of Trade and Commerce was adept at catching it, so the only son was appointed to the board of grain commissioners. If the government had found it necessary to appoint known Liberals to the board of grain commissioners, they could have followed this other policy of appointing men from within the ranks, because Mr. A. G. McLean was fairly well qualified.
In that same regard, as the minister will doubtless point out, they had to increase the salary to attract men to the position. We notice that two of the assistant commissioners are paid $8,500 a year, and the third one, Mr. Rayner, receives $9,000. It looks to me to be a fairly attractive promotion to go up to $12,000 a year, let alone up to $13,500. I do not feel we can entertain for one minute the fact that the salary increase was necessary to attract men to the position, because we find many well qualified men-I am thinking of wheat pool travelling superintendents-who are familiar with every aspect of the Canada Grain Act and who are currently living on a salary of $6,000 to $7,000. I think this principle of reaching beyond your business to fill a position is a very undesirable one. I notice that the Liberal federal government has had to do that three times in recent years in making appointments to the treasury benches. Perhaps they continue the same excuse there, that they could not find amongst their own members anyone capable of filling the position.
In discussing the salary increases of the board of grain commissioners, this police force for the grain industry, I feel it has been amply proven by the hon. member for Assiniboia and the hon. member for Hum-boldt-Melfort that it is the Fearless Fosdicks at the top of the commission who are incompetent and not doing a good job. I do not think we should underestimate the good job that the men working in the service of the board of grain commissioners are doing. When one thinks in terms of men like the chief inspector, the chief chemist and the hundreds of other men who are not in this $12,000 to $14,000 category, but who are receiving incomes of three or four thousand dollars, he realizes that these are the men who are doing an excellent job. I believe they are the ones to whom the hon. member for Fort William was referring when he praised the commissioners. Coming from Fort William, he would assume that the board of grain commissioners were the men doing the work.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext:
I knew what I was talking about.

Canada Grain Act

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext:
I think the hon. member for Fort William made only one mistake, because in the course of his remarks he said that as long as we have the present Minister of Agriculture the farmers of western Canada are going to be well represented. From the evidence I have, I think he meant to use the word "Liberals"-that so long as Liberals are appointed, western Canada will be well represented.
When we investigate the various functions of the board of grain commissioners we find the act states explicitly that:
The commissioners and the assistant grain commissioners shall each ot them devote the whole of his time to the performance of his duties under this act, and shall not accept or hold any other office or employment.
In view of that provision in the act, I am wondering how it is that one of the commissioners holds a full-time job as transport controller. It looks to me as though something is incompatible with the act. The transport controller has the tremendous task of allocating box cars throughout western Canada-indeed throughout Canada as a whole.
On February 4 I inquired from the government as to the number of box cars the C.P.R. and the C.N.R. have. I thought it would be a simple matter to phone the transport controller to get that information. Certainly it did not appear to be top secret. However, in the answer the government said the information was not available. In other words, the man who is responsible for the allocation of box cars at various divisional points in western Canada does not know how many cars these two great railway systems have.
As I pointed out last night, in considering any salary increases at this time one should have in mind the economic conditions in Canada, and should consider the salaries of men who are doing very important jobs in other sections of the economy. Let us look at the salary schedules, and compare them with schedules in other important jobs. We find that Dr. C. H. Goulden, an extremely well qualified man, a man whose services through his rust research have meant millions of dollars to the western farmers, and who has recently been appointed director of experimental farm services, gets $10,500 a year. We see that Dr. K. W. Neatby, another highly qualified and experienced man, receives $11,000 as director of science services. Then, the director of the marketing service receives $10,500 a year.
On the basis of the qualifications of these men, and having in mind the salaries they receive, I do not see why it is necessary to increase the salaries of political appointees on

the board of grain commissioners. I am not: saying for one moment that the salaries of Dr. Goulden, Dr. Neatby and the director of marketing services are high enough-in fact, I think they are too small, in view of the qualifications these men have. But I do say that it would be better to increase salaries at their level, rather than down at the other end of the scale with men whose abilities and qualifications are in doubt.
Lest there be any misconception, let me say that we in this group are in no way critical of the members or the salaries on the Canadian wheat board. They are competent men, and proved themselves so when they appeared before the standing committee on agriculture and colonization. Further, their salaries are paid out of the earnings of the Canadian wheat board and not out of the treasury of Canada, as is proposed in the present instance.
The Canadian wheat board has been of inestimable value to the farmers of western Canada. I maintain that if these policemen of the Canada Grain Act, the board of grain commissioners, had been as efficient as the members of the Canadian wheat board, many of the problems now existing would have disappeared.
As I said at the beginning of my speech, we object to the package deal. We are interested in receiving further information about the first part of the resolution, namely the grading of No. 3 amber Durum wheat and all grades of soybeans. There is not much information on the subject in the resolution. But if the minister insists upon wrapping this up with a rotten ball of twine, and including the annual salaries of the chief and other commissioners, in one case an increase of $1,000 and in the other of $1,500, then we cannot accept that package deal. We must object to it.
If the minister would agree to split the resolution, and introduce it under two separate headings, we would be in a position to act as we think we should on each issue. When this matter comes to a vote we will have to support the farmers of western Canada in their objection to the lack of efficiency in the board of grain commissioners, and their opposition to any increase in salaries at this time. I do not suppose we can expect western Liberals in the House of Commons to vote against this increase.

speechtext: That is right.

speechtext: Because, after the next election, you will be one of the ones looking for the appointment.

speechtext: And that is right.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it had not been my intention to speak on this resolution, because it is in many respects similar to other resolutions we have had dealing with other boards. However, my reason for saying a few words at this time is chiefly because of what was said last night by the hon. member for Assiniboia. And, as a matter of fact, I could include all his colleagues in the C.C.F. party.
They have taken a most unusual attitude, indeed a very strange one. I regret very much that they have chosen to debate the merits of the resolution purely on a basis of personalities. I do not suppose there is anything we can do about those persons with whom the hon. member for Assiniboia and his colleagues fall in love or out of love. That is their privilege. But what they have been saying in that connection has very little relevancy in the discussion on this resolution, as such.
What we are asked to do, and what is involved in the resolution, is to increase the salaries of the commissioners. It does not matter who are the commissioners. Some are commissioners now; they may not be commissioners tomorrow; but the salaries will remain the same. The salary increase is for the board of grain commissioners. We all know-and I think our socialist friends should be the first ones to admit it-that the board of grain commissioners is a very important board. It is looked upon as one of the most important boards in western Canada. For that reason I am surprised that they, since they come from western Canada, should be the ones to oppose this board being placed on the same footing as other important boards in the country. Surely we should be the first ones to approve this resolution to place the members of that board in the same position as other boards, the members of which have received salary increases in the last few years.
I rise particularly to deal briefly with the references that were made yesterday by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) to the sittings of the agriculture committee last year. There again I was very much surprised, because as chairman I understood that everybody had come out of the sittings of the committee last year well pleased with the information that was given there. It is the first time that I have known members to rise in their places and leave the impression, and particularly the hon. member for Assiniboia, that they were not satisfied with the sittings and the findings of the committee last year. There is no question that the evidence given in the committee does not bear out in any way the assertion of the
Canada Grain Act
hon. member for Assiniboia, as recorded in Hansard of yesterday. He referred particularly to the incident of the document and the chairman of the board of grain commissioners. Well, it was one of those things about which there was a little misunderstanding as to the exact identity of the document that was referred to the night before. That happens many times in all committees. As a matter of fact, in that particular case the chairman of the board of grain commissioners had referred to the document previously, so that he was certainly aware that it existed. However, he did not exactly identify it as the one to which the hon. member was referring at that time. The hon. member rises in his place in this house and says that that is clear evidence the chairman of the board of grain commissioners is inefficient and does not know his job. We have to draw the line somewhere. I certainly think it is leaving an entirely wrong impression.
I come now to the other gentleman who was mentioned last night and again today, namely, the transport controller. Reference was made to him and much ado was made about the statement he made in the committee last year. Hon. members who were on the committee will recall that when he made that statement he said that when he was in the grain business-and he was in the grain business many years before he was appointed to the board of grain commissioners -he encountered certain practices. The hon. member for Assiniboia makes a big story out of that and says that he has never encountered it. That is a matter of opinion, if he says he has not and the controller says he has. Many of us know that it has taken place at times. That is the whole point, but it is not within the confines of the act. It is something that has happened. At times some farmers are willing to accept a little lower grade in order to get a little higher price or to get delivery-it would not apply at the present time-of their grain at this time. It is not something that we condone, but the point is it is one of those side instances that do take place.
With respect to the transport controller, I feel very strongly that he has been doing a magnificent job in that capacity ever since his appointment. A very large percentage of the farmers would agree with that statement. They are all aware of what the transport controller has done. They admit that he has done a big job, and we all know that it is a tremendous task. It is not an easy one. He has done it efficiently and with great success.
The hon. member for Assiniboia and a few others might criticize the box car distribution.

Canada Grain Act
We are not supposed to discuss that issue on this resolution, but the whole question was gone into quite thoroughly in the committee. It is fair to say that on that issue there is quite a difference of opinion between the two western provinces. The problem is far more acute in the province in which the hon. member for Assiniboia resides. The evidence shows quite clearly that it is not nearly as acute in the other two provinces, and the situation is quite different. After discussing the whole matter at great length in the committee, we all came to the conclusion that nobody had an acceptable ready solution to the problem. As a matter of fact, the report of the committee so stated and that was the way in which it was presented to the house. Nobody had a ready solution to offer that would be acceptable to the farmers. What was the recommendation in the report? The recommendation in the committee report was simply that we leave the matter in the hands of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to try to work out a solution somehow. When the farmers and the three pools, the Saskatchewan wheat pool, the Manitoba wheat pool and the Alberta wheat pool, which market a very large percentage of the grain in the western provinces, appeared on this very question they also, except possibly Saskatchewan, had no clear-cut suggestion acceptable to all.
The hon. member referred to the overages. I am glad that he did. There is a good illustration of the effective, informative and useful information that was given to the committee last year. All hon. members will recall the numerous discussions that took place in this house up until the time the committee commenced its sittings. All hon. members will also recall that the hon. member for Assiniboia particularly rose in his place in this house again and again and talked on overages and how everybody on the prairies was being robbed on account of overages, and many of his colleagues spoke on the question.

I am satisfied that the committee of last year was more effective than any of the committees in the past, but I may be prejudiced because I was the chairman. However, if anyone will read the evidence I think he will find that all these questions were dealt with quite fully.
During the debate last night and again today reference has been made to the appointment of commissioners, but the resolution before us does not deal with the appointment of a commissioner. There is one assistant commissioner to be appointed. The titles may sound similar but the functions of these two positions are quite different. As I say, the resolution provides for the appointment of one assistant commissioner.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext: For Saskatchewan.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Originally there were three assistant commissioners appointed in order to have one in each province. I understand that the purpose in appointing the extra assistant commissioner is to give Saskatchewan two assistant commissioners.
I am surprised that it should be a socialist hon. member from Saskatchewan who is objecting to the appointment of another assistant commissioner, particularly in view of the remarks made by the hon. member for Kindersley who has just resumed his seat after complaining that the board of grain commissioners had not dealt with the subject matters he had brought to their attention as quickly as he would have liked. With the appointment of another assistant commissioner this objection should be met. I suggest that instead of speaking against the resolution the hon. member should be supporting it.

The whole thing is that at the moment this resolution has nothing to do with personalities. It is simply a question of putting this important board in line with other important boards in the country. I suggest that it is only fair and equitable that we should do it and that it would be in the interests of this important commission that we do it as soon as possible.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution is similar to other resolutions that have been brought in from time to time in that it contains some things which all of us are desirous of securing, but in order to secure those things certain other matters are included with which we are in entire disagreement. In other words, to obtain that which is good we are being asked to swallow a pill of that which is not good.
This resolution divides itself roughly into three parts. The first part has to do with the important export market, as I see it, for Durum wheat which is in demand for the making of macaroni. As the law now stands, grades Nos. 1 and 2 of Durum require confirmation to the best varieties of this brand. In the case of No. 3 an equally good grade can be obtained with a variety less desirable for the making of macaroni.
The amendment simply means that one grade further is advanced. I think that generally this meets the requirements of the farming communities in the western provinces, particularly those which in recent years have gone extensively into the production of Durum wheat. They have done this because of the higher price and because this wheat is not subject to the quota system which is applicable to hard wheat.
Then there is the question of overages, to which the hon. member who has just spoken referred a moment ago. I think the general plan outlined last evening by the senior hon. member for Halifax meets the very serious criticism which has been made in recent years with regard to overages. While the elevator companies in general have been able to say that the percentage actually acquired in overages is very small, the total purchases that were made during the course of the year have amounted to a large sum of money. I remember when in the house in 1951 the late Mr. Fair asked a question to which a return was made which revealed that as between 1945-46 and 1949-50 the net overages in the elevator companies amounted to 9,982,016 bushels of grain, or almost 10 million bushels. Of that total there were 5,621,938 bushels of wheat. In 1945-46, which was the year in which deferred weighovers took place, the amounts in some cases were
Canada Grain Act
nothing short of stupendous. One elevator company showed an overage for that crop year of 800,760 bushels while another showed 434,707 bushels. Those were tremendous overages, and while the explanation may be given that the percentage was small, the amount was fabulous in quantity.
The changes which have been placed before us by the parliamentary assistant are those which have been asked for and they represent to a considerable measure, if not completely, the representations which were made in the committee of last year.
I come now to the general overhauling of the grain act. What I find difficult to understand is the fact that legislation by way of amending an act as important as this one is brought in in a piecemeal fashion and consists of a haphazard system of spasmodic amendments. Farmers in general would like to see the grain act gone into in detail. I believe that there is need for an exhaustive inquiry into the whole question of grain grading, handling, mixing and storage. A thorough study should be made of receipts from farmers and deliveries by companies by grades, and into the condition of all grain purchases since 1945, so that the western farmer in particular may understand the true position.
Such an inquiry could cover such matters as grain inspection and the general practices followed in order to find whether the farmers' interests are being fully protected.
This legislation has been on the statute books for about 43 years. An extensive examination of the statute was made in 1930, but in my opinion the experiences of recent years demand a further extensive consideration. I am not going to suggest a royal commission. The hon. member who just preceded me mentioned the agriculture committee of last year. I was not able to attend at the committee because of my absence from Ottawa at the time.
I read the evidence of that committee and I agree with him that the committee really grappled with the problems before it as few committees have done heretofore. I believe a committee, even the agriculture committee, could go into this matter in detail and examine it closely. This is not a partisan matter. It is a matter which affects the welfare of agriculture in this country in general and the grain producers in western Canada in particular. I believe a committee of parliament could do a tremendous job in conducting an examination of the grain act and in suggesting amendments. There are many hon. members in this house who are desirous of tackling this problem and who would be only too glad to do so but to whom

Canada Grain Act
the opportunity to do the work they are qualified to do is not always available to them because an overwhelming government majority are in opposition.
I think a committee of parliament, or the agriculture committee itself, might undertake this responsible task of dealing with grain handling, grain storage and the general administration of the board. It could also make a study of the effects of large sales of poor grade screenings by elevator companies on the marketing of feed grains in eastern Canada. This is a problem which has been brought to my attention from time to time. It is a problem which could be considered by the members of this house who have the agricultural training and professional knowledge necessary to find a solution. This problem is a matter of everyday concern to them. Out of such an investigation would come not this halting, uncertain, spasmodic type of amendment, but a complete revision of the Canada Grain Act to meet conditions which have changed and which are constantly changing.
Having said that, I now come to a reference to the board of grain commissioners. I feel that that board, and I think I speak for the vast majority of the western farmers in that connection, should have appointed to it representatives of actual farm producers. Indeed, I would go even further and ask for the appointment of trained grain men who could offer valuable and professional advice to the commission. I would ask however for the appointment to that hoard of a majority of farmers.
I do not wish to enter into a criticism of individuals. When a man has served in politics and then received a position on a board he is sometimes subject to criticism. I am going to speak of an individual who was a former member of this house. I refer to John Vallance. John Vallance was a strong and powerful member of this house.

Yes. Mr. Milner is the controller and looks after transportation and that is why I mentioned him in particular. If my right hon. friend would just allow me to develop this thought he would see that it would bear no reference to Mr. Milner other than in a sense of non-criticism. I believe he is trying to do a good job. I must observe, however, that the situation relative to transport control has not been what it should be. When we come to raise the salaries of the members of this board and increase its membership it is natural that the question arises, what appointments are being made? Certainly I believe that any increase in salaries should be delayed. I believe that the appointment of Mr. Loptson is one which cannot conceivably be excused or justified. A producing farmer should be appointed to the board. Mr. Loptson has not been in politics but the appointment has too much resemblance to a political reward given to the son in return for the political activities of his father. No one hearing of that appointment could have any other opinion concerning it when they consider the trained men who are available for that position. I think parliament, and the opposition to the extent it can, should resist a course which is so directly in the nature of a political reward as the case in question. We in Saskatchewan find ourselves in the

position of being forced to conclude that the senior positions in the P.F.R.A. and the P.F.A.A. are positions where Liberal M.P.'s and ex-M.L.A.'s find a place of refuge in their time of need, trouble or defeat. I think the appointment of Mr. Loptson is one which is not justified in the opinion of western farmers in general and it suggests something which one does not want brought into the field represented by the board of grain commissioners.
Reference has been made to Mr. McLean. I do not know anything about his position directly but I do know that the last appointment to the board was one which has caused an unprecedented degree of criticism in the western provinces. I think if the government had really intended to make the board of grain commissioners an efficient and effective body it should have given more consideration to the representations of agriculture in general and western agriculture in particular when the last appointment was made. There are many men who are actually farmers who could have made a valuable contribution to the board.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution refers to a number of matters on some of which there seems to be complete agreement. I think we are all agreed that it is desirable to change the grading of Durum wheat and to return the terminal overages to the wheat board instead of to the treasury as previously provided. There seems to be objection to increasing the salaries of the board of grain commissioners. There has been a general increase in salaries during the last 12 months. Salary increases have been granted to almost every board except the board of grain commissioners, and the purpose of this provision is to do for the board of grain commissioners what has been done for other boards in the service of the federal government, no more and no less. The amount of the increase was approved by treasury board, and there is nothing unusual about that change in the act at this time.
There has been criticism about the work of the board of grain commissioners. It is a strange thing. The board of grain commissioners has many important duties. It has charge of the inspection of wheat. It has charge of protecting wheat in transit from the farmers to the markets abroad. It has charge of the weighing of wheat and of the operation of a chain of terminal elevators. No one has mentioned in what particular the work of the board has been deficient. Certainly the grade standards are the highest in the world. The reason we can sell our wheat while the Americans are giving wheat away is that buyers know the exact type
Canada Grain Act
of wheat they are going to receive when they buy Canadian wheat according to grade, and they are willing to pay a price for that security.
As far as weights are concerned, we had difficulties about weights in the old days having to do with the out-turns of export cargoes. That problem has all disappeared owing to the work of the board. I have heard no recent criticism of the work of the weighing department. I have heard no criticism of the way in which the board operates its terminal elevators. I believe that is an efficient operation. I fail to see how an inefficient board can be efficient in so many directions and I fail to see how an inefficient board can bring the reputation of Canadian wheat in the markets of the world up to the standard it has achieved in this particular year.
Last year I attended a number of the meetings of the committee on agriculture where the efficiency of the board of grain commissioners was discussed. While there I heard every witness say that in his opinion the board of grain commissioners was doing an excellent job. That was said by the presidents of the three wheat pools. It was said by the president of the United Grain Growers and it was said by other witnesses from the grain trade of Canada. There was no difference of opinion there.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce

Perhaps the hon. member for Assiniboia does. I thought I listened very closely to the evidence given before the committee. I have been talking about the work of the board. If my hon. friend will look at the evidence of the witnesses before the committee I think he will see that my statement is correct, that every witness stated that in his opinion the board of grain commissioners is conducting an efficient operation.
There has been criticism of the personnel of the board. One member of the board retired a few days ago because he had reached the statutory age limit, and it was necessary to fill the position. It is my responsibility to fill the position, and in doing so I asked for advice. I wrote to the three producer grain companies operating in Saskatchewan and

Canada Grain Act
asked for recommendations. I obtained three recommendations from the Saskatchewan wheat pool. The pool recommended three men each of whom was a director of a wheat pool. The United Grain Growers recommended a director of that company who had been a director for eight years, I believe. The farmers union also recommended a person who was not a director of that organization.
Each of the five men was very carefully investigated. I had reports on all of them from people whom I consider to be reliable witnesses. I thought a basic requirement was that a member of the board of grain commissioners should be an actual wheat producer; in other words, a dirt farmer. I am told today that we should have filled the vacancy by promotion from within the board, by moving up a member of the staff of the board. That is a new thought. I have never heard that demand from the prairies. I thought I had heard them all but that is a new variety.
I looked into the qualifications of Mr. Loptson. I took into account the fact that he had been a farmer all his life, that he farmed 1,750 acres of land. May I say to my hon. friends who speak so freely of their farming experience that that is a sizeable farm. I should think it would amount to about the aggregate acreage farmed by all those in the group of men who have been discussing this particular measure.

Let us not be ridiculous. I do not mind fair debate, but when we hear it sai'd that because a man has served as a Liberal member in the provincial parliament his son must naturally be a Liberal and that the appointment of his son is a reward to the father, may I venture to say that the son is probably much better off than his father and well able to stand on his own feet. Let us not take that argument quite as seriously as it has been presented today.
It is said that the Liberal party never makes an appointment without taking care of a Liberal. I have noticed particularly that when any member of the C.C.F. party leaves the House of Commons he is subsequently found in the employment of the C.C.F. government of Saskatchewan. There are men in the house now who were previously defeated, were then in the employ of the provincial government of Saskatchewan, and are now back in the House of Commons. That is all right, but let us not be-

-too pure about matters of that kind. I do not know that I need to say anything further. The hon. member for Calgary North seemed a little confused. He was discussing the appointment of an assistant commissioner to the board as another member of the board. He criticized the fact that this man was to be appointed for Saskatchewan. As has been said in the course of the debate, there are three assistant commissioners on the board, one for Alberta, one for Saskatchewan and one for Manitoba. The fact of the matter is that over half of the wheat from the prairies is grown in Saskatchewan and the number of country elevators in Saskatchewan is about twice the number of country elevators in either of the other two provinces.
The board of grain commissioners has represented to me that one assistant commissioner in Saskatchewan could not do the job adequately. He just could not visit all the country elevators in rotation, as he should, within 12 months. The proposal, therefore, is to divide Saskatchewan into two districts and appoint a second grain commissioner to cover the new territory. I think, Mr. Chairman, that the discussion of the details

of the bill should wait until we have a copy of the bill. That is all I have to say at the moment.

speechtext:
While we are discussing
personalities, I should like to announce to the house that the Campbell rink from Avon-lea has won the Canadian championship for curling. They have won by going through the competition without a defeat.
While I am on my feet, I should like to corroborate what has been said by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. He indicated a while ago that he did not know Mr. Loptson was a son of the Mr. Loptson who has been, not leader of the Liberal party at any time as was said last night, but who was appointed house leader for one session. He has never been at any time leader of the Liberal party. I wanted to say, too, that the minister did not know that this gentleman came from my constituency, as he does. I believe that should answer some of the suggestions which have been made. As a matter of fact, I came into the house the day after the appointment was made and congratulated the minister across the aisle on having made the first appointment of this kind from my constituency in the 20 years I have been here. I believe I could name several very important appointments that have been made from the constituencies of hon. members on the other side of the house, particularly the C.C.F. party.
These appointments of persons who have been in politics before are quite natural. I would hope that the provincial government in Saskatchewan was acting on the same reasons as Liberals and Conservatives have in the past when making appointments of exmembers. I believe we have learned from association with these members what their worth actually is. We are making use of the experience these men have gained while they have been members of this house. I could name two or three well known members of the C.C.F. party who, when they left this house as a result of defeat, went back to Saskatchewan and obtained positions with the Saskatchewan government for anywhere from 12 months to 2 or 3 years. Two of them have actually been taken into the Saskatchewan government after going back there. This sort of action is not taken by one party any differently from any other party. Then, I see two of them who were defeated on one occasion sitting over there in one seat. One of them took a job with the Saskatchewan government between elections until he got back here, and the other one had a first-class job with the C.C.F. party while he was waiting to get back again. I do not know
Canada Grain Act
that we are going to get anywhere discussing that sort of thing in relation to appointments of this kind.
I doubt if there is a single man on the other side of the house who even knows Mr. Loptson. If he had been politically active, I should like to know why they do not know him. My reason for saying that is that I have not heard a single one of them refer to him by the name by which he is known. He is not known as Stanley Loptson out in Saskatchewan. When it comes to talking about experience emphasis has been placed on the fact that he is the only son of the Mr. Loptson who was, for one session, the house leader in Saskatchewan; that has been played up. Well, he is the only son of a man who was one of the most successful farmers in western Canada and, as a matter of fact, one of the most successful Icelandic settlers in western Canada. The son has been with his father throughout his whole lifetime. They have managed 1,750 acres over the years. They have produced farm commodities of a kind that has led others into the production of such things as rape seed and other forms of farm production in greater numbers perhaps than any other farmer. They are mixed farmers. They produce livestock as well as wheat. In addition to that he has sufficient ability to run two hardware stores, one in Saskatchewan and one in Manitoba, and run them successfully. He has also run a first-class garage. If a man can do all those things as successfully as he has and yet is not capable of filling a position of this kind, I should like to know what is to be said for members of this house who, when they are defeated and go back home, cannot make a living without getting a job from the Saskatchewan government.
This man is comparatively young, he is in his 40's. He was not suggested by anyone who had any political axe to grind. He was suggested by the president of the United Grain Growers. What is the United Grain Growers? The United Grain Growers is a farmers' cooperative that was set up by the first farm organization we had in western Canada since we started growing wheat. It was a company set up by Mr. E. A. Partridge, who was the originator of the idea of having a board such as we have been talking about. The old Grain Growers Grain Company first suggested a board of grain commissioners around the beginning of the century, under the Manitoba grain act, and brought into being the farm co-operative organizational life of western Canada. It was Mr. E. A. Partridge of Sintaluta who started the organization of the United Grain Growers in that town. It was made up entirely of farmers. The co-operative has gone on from that time up to the moment

Canada Grain Act
I think it covers all three of the provinces with its elevators and farm organizations. It is the original co-operative in western Canada. While the pools have been growing up, while establishments such as the Saskatchewan co-operative elevator company and others have grown up in the province, the United Grain Growers has grown up and functioned right alongside of them. It was this organization that suggested Mr. Loptson to the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
As the minister said, it was after he had decided to appoint Mr. Loptson that he learned Mr. Loptson had some relationship to a member of the Saskatchewan legislature. I know that he learned it then because it was in a conversation with me after he had decided to appoint him. I suggested to him, "Well, you know who he is." He said, "No, I do not know who he is, but I know what his qualifications are from the representations I have received from the United Grain Growers." Of course, I told him he was the son of a member of the Saskatchewan legislature, but that did not result in the minister not appointing him. I presume if I had said to him he is not a fit person to appoint because he is a Liberal, well, he would not have appointed him. Even if I had said he was not a fit person because he was a member of the Saskatchewan farmers union, he would not have refused to appoint him. He is an active paid-up member of the farmers' union and has been working on that continuously. He is not a person who comes to the house and says, "I am all for the farmers, because the farmers are the greater number of voters in my constituency." He is a man who has been a farmer, and made money from it. And then he invested some of what he made in other activities, and was successful in everything he touched.
Then, he has been a member of the board of United Grain Growers now for six years. I knew nothing at all about his capabilities as a grain operator. I would not have thought of proposing him as a member of the grain board, from any knowledge I had. But when the president of United Grain Growers, the old original company, said, "We have had him six years and we want him put on the board", and then when the whole board of United Grain Growers met-not in Saskatchewan, but in Calgary-and unanimously passed a resolution that they wanted him, then all I wish to say to this house and to anyone else interested in it is that so far as I am concerned I would be as much influenced by the opinion of the board of United Grain Growers as by any of the other farm boards. I would not be any more influenced by this board than I am by the opinion of other farm boards.

Now, I am going to say this, so far as Mr. Loptson is concerned-and I know him as well as any member in the house knows him- I know him as a successful businessman and as a successful farmer and as a man who is a hard worker and who will give all his time and skill to this particular job, just as much as he has given to his own business and his own farming. I am sure that he will make a success of it. I would not be at all surprised if the same members-if they are allowed to sit here long enough to find out- who have been criticizing him here today, will be saying, "Well, we did not know him, after all; he has done a good job." speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first of all I wish to associate myself with the remarks of the Minister of Agriculture in congratulating the Campbell brothers of Avonlea, Saskatchewan, upon winning the Macdonald Brier trophy, and on becoming Canada's curling champions. It is particularly fitting that this trophy should come to Saskatchewan, which this year is celebrating her fiftieth anniversary. Perhaps I might be pardoned for injecting a personal note in stating that I had the privilege and honour of attending Avonlea public and high schools with all the Campbell brothers-Garnet, Don, Glen, Lloyd and Gordon. There are five brothers, and a combination of four of these brothers has made a championship rink.
They are all farmers, and that is something else I wish to point out. The skip, the youngest of the brothers, is just 28 years of

age, a graduate of Avonlea high school, and is now farming. Don, the man playing third, joined the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. But he decided to exchange his position in the R.C.M.P. for the occupation of farming, and went back to farm in association with his brother Lloyd. Glen, who plays second, is a chartered accountant, a graduate of the University of Saskatchewan. He, too, decided to return to the Avonlea district and farm. Lloyd, who plays lead, is the most extensive farmer of the Campbell brothers. And because he had such large holdings his brothers Don and Glen gave up responsible positions to become associated with him as farmers.
The fifth brother, Gordon, who is not on this team but who has often appeared on Campbell brothers curling teams, and who ranks as a curler with his brothers, is an engineer, a graduate of the University of Saskatchewan. He, too, decided to make farming his lifework. I think it is most fitting that the honoured and respected Campbell brothers of Avonlea, Saskatchewan, should be Canada's 1955 curling champions.
I wish to refer now to the information given the house by the Minister of Trade and Commerce when he referred to the recommendations made to him as to those who might be suitable for appointment to the board of grain commissioners. If I heard the minister correctly, he said that the Saskatchewan wheat pool had made three recommendations, and that the three men recommended were all directors of the pool. He said that the United Grain Growers had recommended directors of that organization, and that the farmers union-presumably the Saskatchewan farmers union-had also recommended a man for the position.
I think it is a real affront to western farm organizations that the man who was appointed to the board of grain commissioners did not come from either the wheat pool organization or the farmers union. It is true that the United Grain Growers is a farm organization, of a type.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES

There is a way out, as I have said. It is for the government to appoint a man who has been recommended by the farmers' unions.
The Minister of Agriculture mentioned the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. Well, of course some of the main organizations that go to make up the Canadian Federation of Agriculture are the three western wheat pool organizations. I am sure that the president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool and Dr. Hannam, head of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, could agree quite readily on the person that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, representing the three western pools, would recommend as a member of the board of grain commissioners.
The minister said there was no evidence before the agriculture committee that there was any inefficiency. The heads of the grain companies had said that grade standards were good and the practices followed under the Canada Grain Act were reasonably good. But we had-and the minister saw this himself-the board of grain commissioners unable to give adequate information, unable to explain, for example, why net overages happened to be in many instances three times or four times as much as gross overages. I had no idea as to how that would come about, and the members of the board of grain commissioners could not explain it. But some time later I happened to have lunch with Mr. G. A. Mills, who is president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool employees' association He pointed out to me how such a thing could happen. It was very simple after he had explained it to me. For example, he said if an elevator agent is buying No. 3 barley and in it there is too much wheat, that wheat could be cleaned out and it would go into the wheat bins and increase the net overages of wheat. It would have no effect, as I understood the explanation, on the gross overages at all. He went on to explain other

methods by which net overages could exceed gross overages. When the board of grain commissioners were asked about it they could not explain it. The only explanation given was this. It may at best have been a facetious remark, because surely Mr. Milner would know better. He said probably the reason why most of those overages came about was that the elevator agents were taking excessive dockage in exchange for upgrading of grain.
I listened with a great deal of interest to the speech made this afternoon by the hon. member for Provencher. If I took down his words correctly he said that at no time did he hear it said that such a practice was done within the confines of the act. If he had read the answer given by Mr. Milner at page 256 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the committee in relation to a hypothetical question by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek he would have known differently. The hon. member asked this question:
Is there anything in the Canada Grain Act which would prevent me, if I took in a load of grain, thinking it was No. 4 and the elevator man thinks it is No. 5? The majority of farmers like to see their elevator men at the end of the year come out even. They do not like to see overages or shortages. They endeavour not to place him in a short position, so therefore they are inclined to compromise on the grade. He may think it is No. 5 while I think it is No. 4. We discuss the matter and if he allows me a grade and it is marginal grade, I may be aware that it is a marginal grade, and he will say: I will allow that as No. 4 while I think it is No. 5, but I will do so if I may have additional dockage. I may have to take less than I ordinarily would but if I do not object to it and am of the opinion that I may lose a grade in that way I will accept it. What is wrong with that?

That being the case, when the government are appointing a new person to the board of grain commissioners I think they should take the largest agricultural organizations in western Canada into their confidence and appoint a man only if he has the recommendation of at least one of the two main organizations. The time may come when the salaries of the board of grain commissioners should be increased. Mr. Chairman, coming as I do from the curling province of Canada I should like to add my congratulations to those which have been extended to the Avonlea curling team upon their recent victory. They must be good to have beaten Manitoba and they deserve it.
I welcome the announcement by the minister that the recommendations contained in

Canada Grain Act
the report of the committee regarding terminal overages will be carried out by means of an amendment to the act. With regard to the appointment of an assistant commissioner, the need for such appointment was indicated in the evidence given before the committee last year. I believe that this appointment will fill a definite need.
A recent appointment to the board of grain commissioners was that of a practical farmer, the type of appointment which has been asked for by the farm organizations over the past years. This man appears to be capable and efficient and he has made a success in his own affairs. I do not think that any appointment made by the government would meet with the approval of our friends to my left.
I had no intention of entering this debate until I heard in this house an unjustified attack on the Canada Grain Act and on the personnel and operations of the board of grain commissioners. It is to this phase of the matter that I intend to direct my attention.
Along with hon. members to my left I sat on the agriculture committee last year and my over-all impression was that the board was doing a very good job. Naturally my impression did not agree with that expressed by other hon. members during this debate. I feel that in their destructive statements the C.C.F. members are not doing a service to the farmers of Canada by unjustly undermining their confidence in the board of grain commissioners.
As I said before, I sat on the committee. As my memory did not recall sufficient incidents to support the statements made in this debate I took the trouble to examine the evidence to see what the representatives of the various farm organizations, who also sat through the hearings, thought of this particular board. I was not surprised to find that their opinions differed entirely from those expressed in the speeches made in this house and I thought that in all fairness they should be put on the record.
The evidence given by Ben S. Plumer, president of the Alberta wheat board, appears at page 400 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the committee, where he is reported as having said:
We have no particular comment to make on those reports other than to congratulate both boards on the outstanding services which they have contributed to the grain producers of western Canada, especially over the past few years when record crops have been produced.
And then at page 408 he had this to say:
We believe that the Canada Grain Act, competently administered as it is, by the board of grain commissioners provides ample protection for the producer in assuring him of accuracy in weights, grades and dockages, to conform as closely as possible to government standards.

Then on page 457 we find Mr. Bill Parker, president of the Manitoba pool elevator association, being examined by the hon. member for Lisgar as to whether he agreed that tens of thousands of farmers had lost confidence in the board of grain commissioners. Mr. Parker then went on to say: From my own observation, I would say that is not a fact and I speak particularly for Manitoba. If I may, I would like to read two or three resolutions that we had last year in response to requests for information that were sent out to the locals in the country. On February 23, 1953, the farmers' unions of the three provinces made a presentation in Winnipeg to the board of grain commissioners and on the following day they made a presentation to the wheat board. These were public presentations. It was given to the press in full and some of us felt that the publicity given to it gave undue emphasis to criticisms, which we felt, rightly or wrongly, were not entirely justified. Having in mind that the farm organizations for 40 years have worked towards the provisions of the Canada Grain Act and have always been interested in its administration, and more recently intensely interested in the operation of the Canadian wheat board. Frankly, Mr. Chairman, we were greatly disturbed at the publicity given. We sent these briefs to our locals, asking if they would be good enough to consider them and give us their opinions. We have answers from 80 of the 208 or 209 locals. Those that did not answer, you can make your own interpretation as to their reactions. Four of those associations did support in some measure the contentions or criticisms embodied in those briefs. Only one supported them unconditionally. Incidentally, that one is an association which had not yet considered an annual report, and their knowledge of the grain business is, to say the least, rather meager. Three of them were older and had been in the business for some time and they did feel there was some justification for some of the criticisms. If I can find it here I would like to read you one or two resolutions, which go for the vast majority that did answer and make comments on the briefs. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that they were constructive, they were made by people who were in the business 15 to 25 years, who really had some knowledge of both acts and of the administrative boards in both capacities. This is the answer from the Kronsgart association in southeastern Manitoba:
"That since the whole tone and content of the two briefs in question tend to weaken confidence in these boards and thus impair their efficiency, and since farmers, through their own organizations, have striven for many years to bring these boards into existence, and since it is evident that they have and are doing a difficult job efficiently, we wish to counteract, in some measure, the adverse influence in the two briefs in question by expressing our full confidence in both the board of grain commissioners and the Canadian wheat board." From the basswood association in the central western part of the province:
That the arguments contained in the M.F.U. briefs do not represent the views of this board of directors, and that we are pretty well satisfied with the operation of the two boards.
Just one other, from the Fairfax association in the southwestern part of the province:
After a very lengthy study and discussion on the M.F.U. submissions to the Canadian wheat board and the board of grain commissioners, this board of directors of Fairfax co-operative elevator were of the unanimous opinion that the present wheat board and board of grain commissioners are doing a satisfactory job under present conditions.

We consider many of the submissions of the M.F.U. are childish and impossible; they are attractive but impractical.
Now I repeat that those resolutions are representative of all answers received, excepting only four. These answers quoted and others in different language and in different resolutions fairly well indicate the opinion of those who did take the trouble to answer and consider the briefs; three others supported some parts of the criticism. That, sir, is the best answer I can give you to the question.
Speaking later on in regard to the same matter he had this to say;
I think in respect to the weighing in the gross that there is protection under the Canada Grain Act; and so far as I am aware the board has administered the act in respect thereto in the interest of the farmer.
Now, in respect to grading, the board or the act does not contemplate that there shall be an inspector at every country elevator. Getting correct grade and dockage is the farmer's own responsibility, as I said yesterday; and if he is not satisfied with the grade and the dockage, or if he has any doubts in the world about the dockage, or about the grade, our instructions are never to argue with the farmer. The farmer is always right so far as the elevator agent is concerned. And there are provisions under which he may take a sample which should be representative of the load of grain concerned; and there is a sample box provided for each farmer, and he can get it and put the sample in it and send it to the board of grain commissioners chief inspector, and his grading is final.
The farmer must exercise some responsibility in respect to his own grades. Surely, he does not expect the government or the board to protect him at every turn.
The act, in my opinion, gives full protection to the individual farmer, provided he reads the act and uses it. So far as our association is concerned, we have spent a lot of time trying to persuade or trying to have the farmers understand what their own personal rights are and that they should exercise them to the full. That is the best answer I can give you.
In the evidence given by Mr. Cecil Lamont, president, North-West Line Elevators Association, at page 490 of the report, the following appears:
I would like here to refer to an action taken by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. This is an official statement issued by Roy C. Marler, chairman of the prairie section of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. I quote from this statement:
The prairie section of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture met in Regina on Wednesday, June 10, 1953. The meeting discussed a number of problems affecting western agriculture, such as the international wheat agreement, freight rates on grain and the sale of coarse grains by the Canadian wheat board.
The following resolution was passed unanimously: Resolved that this section declare its confidence in the personnel of the board of grain commissioners and the Canadian wheat board and the administration these boards are giving their respective acts. The Canada Grain Act has been built up over the years by the constant efforts of the farm organizations to protect the interests of western farmers. As now framed the act does afford the protection for which these organizations had hoped. The western section has every confidence 50433-123J
Canada Grain Act
that any comprehensive study of the act will show that no extensive revisions are necessary at this time.
A resolution was passed also expressing appreciation and confidence in R. Milner and his work as transport controller.	,
Well, we are not members of this Canadian Federation of Agriculture. We follow its work, and we are in full accord with this resolution in all respects.
These, Mr. Chairman, are the opinions of the presidents of the Manitoba and Alberta pools, of Manitoba locals and of the federation of agriculture, all representative and speaking for the grain producer without motive or prejudice. The president of the Saskatchewan pool had no real criticism except for the matter of box car allocation, which in my opinion would indicate that he was in agreement with the opinion I have just quoted. These men and the organizations they represent are responsible bodies with more experience individually than can be found collectively on the C.C.F. benches, and I would be inclined to accept their opinions in preference to those given by/ people who seek to foster political issues*

speechtext:
I perhaps should not project myself into this debate this afternoon, and I am a little reluctant to do so in that I have not been a member of the committee on agriculture and colonization which has devoted a great deal of time to the study of grain marketing matters in recent years. However, it is interesting to note the difference in emphasis placed on the matter of grain handling today as compared with the situation some 20 or 25 years ago.
I shall claim no credit for having dealt extensively in the grain producing business. Nevertheless, I can look back to my boyhood days when I delivered grain to elevators and note the change which has taken place since that time. I wish to deal, however, with the farm movement generally and the time when it was more particularly concerned with two features of grain marketing. One was the out-turn standards from terminal elevators, and the other was the control over any overages which might accumulate in terminal elevators.
These two matters have been rather effectively taken care of, and as the Minister of Trade and Commerce indicated this afternoon our out-turn sample or standard is now recognized throughout the world on our final certificate as the quality and grade of grain which was delivered and which has been accepted on that basis. As a result of this Canadian grain sold on the standard enjoys a considerable and a sound reputation. Similarly, the control of overages at terminal

Canada Grain Act
elevators has also been taken care of, largely through the provision for the confiscation of overages over a certain percentage.
Since the period before the 1920's the problem ' has drifted back more and more to the local elevators, and new problems have developed in this connection. One of the chief difficulties in recent years in the handling of grain, if there have been difficulties, has been the congestion, the inability of country elevators to handle grain in a normal and ordinary way as they would if there were not congested conditions. I think each of us will admit that it is not possible for even the best equipped elevators to give the type of service the elevator companies would like to give. Nonetheless I think every elevator company and elevator agent endeavours to give the best service possible.
I would like to re-emphasize the statement by the hon. member for Springfield to the effect that the Canada Grain Act places the responsibility, yes, and the authority and the right, on the farmer to a larger extent than is apparently accepted by members of the C.C.F. group. When a farmer delivers grain to an elevator it is a situation involving two individuals. There can easily be a difference of opinion as to what grade or dockage a particular sample of grain may carry. I do not need to tell hon. members who have operated combines that one may get an entirely different sample of grain from either side of the same field.
Second, this is a matter involving a particular product which concerns two individuals. If these two individuals, the farmer and the elevator man, can agree as to the grade and dockage the sample of grain should have, there need be no further argument. Settlement is made and the ticket is issued on that basis. That is the agreement and arrangement made between them. More than that, my friends talk so much about dockage. In our country we have now got to the stage where we have plenty of dockage of grain. I am amazed sometimes that the elevator companies are able to break even because of the amount of dockage in much of the grain in some areas of my own district. I will limit it to that for fear I get into trouble if I go beyond that.
As far as dockage is concerned, every elevator man today is provided with a set of screens of the same calibre and size as are used at terminal elevators. The farmer delivering his grain has a right to have it weighed and measured and the weight established per measured bushel. He can have it screened right in front of him and the dockage calculated. He has the opportunity of seeing that for himself. That operation is

done mechanically, and there can be little argument about it. There may be an argument as to grade, but there should be no argument with respect to dockage when it is established in that manner.
Again, the farmer can accept the grade or dockage or he can say, "No, I do not want to take it. I am going to ask you to load out this grain or take it in"-whichever he likes -"and send a sample to the board of grain commissioners to have it graded there". That is his privilege, and he can require the elevator agent to take a uniform sample out of the load of grain delivered. He can see that it is properly mixed and put in a container with a lock on it, and he can carry the key away with him. The sample is then sent to the board as his sample and is graded officially by the officials of the board of grain commissioners. That of course is final.
Compare that with other types of grading. Take the case of the man who delivers a hog to a packing house. It is graded by a government grader. That grade is final and there is no recourse from it. But the farmer delivering grain can have it graded at the local elevator, and if he does not like the grade he does not need to accept it. When his car of grain goes through Winnipeg and the board of grain commissioners arranges for a sample to be taken from the car the farmer may find some difference in the grade from what the local elevator man was prepared to give him. He still has recourse to a sample of the grain taken at unloading. In most elevators that is done by an automatic mechanical sampler, which guarantees a uniform sample out of the whole carload of grain. When that is done and tests are made the farmer has some assurance that it will be properly examined and a mechanical test made of the dockage. I presume they have good mathematicians to figure out what percentage of dockage applies to that delivery of grain.
I emphasize again, notwithstanding all the arguments other people advance to the effect that there is something wrong in the marketing of grain or the administration of the Canada Grain Act, that I think they are making a mistake in not impressing more and more on the individual the rights he has under the existing legislation. He has his part to play in seeing that he gets what he is entitled to, and provision is made for him to get it.
I am not going to say anything more about that feature of the matter. But I must say that I cannot sit here this afternoon and listen to what to my mind is pretty much, if not entirely, an attack of a personal character on individual members of the board of grain commissioners without making some

reply. I do not mind saying that I am personally interested in that I have known all the members of the board for a long time. I was very glad to see the hon. member for Prince Albert stand up and say what he did this afternoon about one member of the board who was at one time a member of the House of Commons.
My hon. friends in the C.C.F. group keep coming back and emphasizing the point of view that the only persons who should be appointed to boards of this nature are dirt farmers. I do not do anything else but dirt farm when I am not attending the House of Commons, and if I were turned out to pasture from here tomorrow there would be no other place for me to go but back to the farm.
I want to say something about the background-and I do so deliberately-of the members of the board of grain commissioners as I have known them. I think I can disabuse the mind of any reasonable person in the house as to their affiliation, their close connection and their background in the farm movement of western Canada. In referring to a more recent appointment to the board of grain commissioners the Minister of Agriculture mentioned Mr. Partridge, one of the early pioneers in the farmers movement of western Canada. I think he was the gentleman who was perhaps more responsible than anyone else for creating the point of view in the farmers' movement generally that the manner in which they could remedy many of their difficulties was to get into the business for themselves.
The other man associated with him in that effort was the late Roderick McKenzie of Brandon, Manitoba, one of the active members of the early farm movement in this country, a man who was secretary of the farm movement in the province of Manitoba in the early days, the father of D. G. McKenzie, the present chairman of the board of grain commissioners. For years the present chairman acted as his father's assistant in stamping, sealing and mailing letters all over the country. He was also secretary of the united farmers of Manitoba for a number of years and was, I believe, a member of the Canadian council of agriculture which represented the farmers of western Canada in the 1920's.
That may not be enough for some hon. members as to the background and approach to his duties, if you like, of this man. It is true that Mr. McKenzie entered politics in the province of Manitoba, where he made a real contribution. He was almost commandeered to take office. What positions did he hold in the government of Manitoba? At
Canada Grain Act
one time he had charge of our hydroelectric power commission, and was responsible for developing the policy that has done more than anything else that has happened in our province to bring rural electrification to the farms of Manitoba. He was responsible for initiating the policy that is the pride of every farmer in that province.
Not only that, he was also minister of agriculture. I suppose my hon. friends will say that as minister of agriculture he did not come in contact with the farmers at all, that his position had nothing to do with the farm movement and he was removed entirely from it. My hon. friends talk about the background of persons entitling them to appointments of this character, but I am at a loss from what they say to know what kind of background a man should have.
I might also say a word about my very good friend of long standing who was at one time my guide and director in the House of Commons, when I first came here in the 1930's. I refer to John Vallance. He was an immigrant. He came to our province and then went to Saskatchewan. I know something of his early history. While he may have been a little more fortunate than the hon. member for Maple Creek, whose family did not have a place for him to move into when he was born, Mr. Vallance actually lived in a sod shanty on the plains of Saskatchewan for a number of years. He homesteaded there. He grew up there. I believe he was the first reeve of the first municipality organized in that area. He was part of the farm movement there, and farmed extensively in that province. Then he came down here as a member of parliament; from Scottish immigrant boy to a member of the House of Commons of Canada.
He fell by the wayside in a political contest and, if my memory serves me right, took a position as assistant commissioner under the Canada Grain Act in Saskatchewan. I would think that would certainly give a man a very good point of view. He was in touch with elevator agents and with farmers, and I think that would fit him in a creditable manner for appointment to the board of grain commissioners.
There is one other thing I think hon. members have overlooked in so far as Mr. Vallance is concerned. There is no one here on any side of the house who has made a closer study of, or paid more attention to, the Canada Grain Act than has John Vallance. He was here before 1930 when there were a good many arguments over the grain act. He was one of the most active members in the complete revision, either in 1930 or in 1928, of that act. I do not think there is any

Canada Grain Act
person who has any better insight into the whys and wherefores of the different sections of the Canada Grain Act.
I am not well acquainted with Mr. Milner, but I am going to say this to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I think he was particularly fortunate in being able to select a man of Mr. Milner's capacity and background of experience to join the board of grain commissioners. He is a man experienced in the grain trade, who successfully operated elevators of his own. If that is to condemn a man for the position of administrator on a board having to do with the marketing of grain, then I think it is too bad for us. As the Minister of Trade and Commerce suggested here this afternoon, the board not only administers the Canada Grain Act but it also has to administer a number of terminal elevators which the government owns. I feel the minister is to be commended for going out and attempting to secure a man to come on this board who has had some practical experience in the operation of elevators.
Now, Mr. Chairman, perhaps I am guilty of something not very many members do in coming to the defence of people in the manner in which I have. But I have felt that the attacks which have been made on the board of grain commissioners over some years now, even to the point of singling them out individually, have been wholly unfair and wholly uncalled for, and I welcome this opportunity to say what I have said.
