speechtext:
It had not been my intention, Mr. Chairman, to take part in this debate. I do so only briefly, and my decision to take part in it at all can be attributed to some of the remarks I have heard in the last couple of hours and the attitude taken in this debate by my friends in the C.C.F. concerning these supposed political appointments. I am very surprised to hear them take that attitude. It is a well-known saying that those in glass houses should not throw stones. I do not know of any group that lives in a house containing more glass than my hon. friends opposite. I possibly could go into quite a few instances, but I shall just take the odd one.
The Minister of Agriculture pointed to a couple of gentlemen who rather give the lie to the idea that no political appointments are made by the C.C.F. Perhaps it would be well to take a look at the record of our knights in shining armour over there. If we go back to 1944, I have a newspaper clipping here quoting the leader of the C.C.F. in this house. In the city of Saskatoon, on June 9, 1944, he is reported to have said:
The day of the political heeler in Saskatchewan will be at an end If the C.C.F. is elected. Mr. Coldwell promised.
fMr. Weir.]
I think you will remember my remarks last year-

speechtext:
When there is talk about political appointments, then I think we should cite some made by hon. members sitting opposite me. I shall deal with one in particular, and let it go at that. We had in the House of Commons at one time a gentleman by the name of Bentley, who was known to my hon. friends. When he went back to Saskatchewan there was no job open for him in the C.C.F. government there, so they made one. His title then was director of staff training. That is rather interesting, if one just goes by the
Canada Grain Act
title. However I had some experience with this staff training. One of the first things he did was to address letters to all ministers in the government of Saskatchewan. His letter, dated August 9, 1949, was in these words:
Re Field Officers
Would you please supply me with the names ol all the field officers in your department, together with their addresses, and the areas in which they work-by constituencies, if possible.
That was the work of this gentleman. It indicates the kind of work he was doing, and it is certainly a lot different from the appointment to the board we are now discussing.
I have still to meet the gentleman who has been appointed in this instance, although he lives in Saskatchewan. So I do not think he is very active politically. I have also run into some of the field officers trained by my friend Mr. Bentley, and I must say he is a good trainer. Last election I got into one poll after one of his well-trained field officers had been to see the farmers in that area, and had toh' them that if they did not have a C.C.F. majority at that poll the hay leases would change hands.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext: Are you talking about P.F.R.A.?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext: You do not like it, eh? Then what happened?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GRADES, ASSISTANT COMMISSIONERS AND SALARIES
speechtext: Name him.

speechtext:
The result was that some of my own Liberals came to me and said that they were going to vote to make sure there was a C.C.F. majority at that poll, and there was.
Then in another poll, just adjacent to it the returning officer had difficulty in getting people to serve at the poll. They were afraid of the repercussions that might develop in that area in connection with hay leases. That is the kind of thing we are getting in Saskatchewan. So it is odd to hear my hon. friends taking exception to what they suggest is a political flavour in this particular appointment.
I believe what I have said covers the situation fairly well. Certainly if the gentleman appointed in this instance had been very active in Liberal circles I would have met him and, as I have said, I have yet to see him.
Then, in common with the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa, I take exception to the personal attack made by hon. members against the grain commissioners. These men have proved satisfactory; and just because in the odd case they have been connected with politics, or have been Liberals, that should not be held against them. Certainly if we are to take the qualification laid down by the hon. member for Kindersley, that the

Canada Grain Act
appointment should go to the best man for the job-and I am not disagreeing with him in that-then naturally there will be more Liberals appointed than anything else. That would be true if for no reason other than that of mathematics, because there are more Liberals than anything else.
I am suggesting that we should not take the judgment of the hon. member for Kindersley, because he made one speech in Saskatchewan in which he said that he saw no one having intelligence on this side of the house.

speechtext:
Yes, I will. I am very well acquainted with the London and Port Stanley railway, Mr. Speaker, and the difficulty the city of London and the London railway commission have encountered over the years. The explanatory notes in the bill are very complete, and I think any further explanation need only be a brief one. The London and Port Stanley railway is an electrified line carrying freight and passengers between London and Port Stanley on lake Erie, a total distance of some 25 miles. Since 1914 the railway has been operated by the London railway commission as agent for the city of London under a 99-year lease from the railway company.
The city is the holder of 95 per cent of the common stock and of ail of the bonds which have been issued from time to time to finance the operation. The bonds have been in default for both principal and interest for many years and greatly exceed the value of the railway assets, so there is no equity for any shareholders.
The effect of this bill and the agreement which it ratifies is to transfer the assets of the railway to the city and extinguish the liability of the railway company, which will simplify the operation of the railway.
In the bill there is quite a long explanatory note which sets forth the history of the company over a long period of years. I know the difficulty the city has encountered in financing, managing and handling the affairs of the company. This bill is to simplify the whole procedure so far as the city of London, the railway commission and the public utilities commission are concerned.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 232, respecting the Bonaventure and Gaspe Telephone Company Limited.
(Translation):
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill concerns the Bonaventure and Gaspe Telephone Company^ Limited. This company, established in 1907, operates mainly in the province of Quebec, particularly in Bonaventure and Gaspe counties.
For this reason it is felt desirable to have the name in French as well as in English, as is provided in the bill.
The company also requests authority to increase its capital stock from $100,000, divided into shares of $100 each, to $2 million, divided into shares of a par value of $25 each.
The capital sum required for the operation of a small local telephone system a half century ago is no longer adequate to meet the necessities of a territory which is now undergoing a great economic expansion and whose

population has been in need of better and enlarged telephone communications for a long time.
This telephone company is now faced with growing demands for better equipment and extension of its facilities to individuals, as well as to several communities which are deprived of adequate communication in Bonaventure and Gaspe counties.
All other powers requested by the company through this bill are necessary to any telephone company that wishes to extend its services and are normally granted to telephone companies operating in this country.
The counties of Bonaventure and Gaspe are on the eve of unprecedented industrial progress, thanks to their rich mineral resources whose development is only now getting under way.
Two of the main factors which have so far delayed the normal development of this scenic part of the province of Quebec are on the one hand the lack of adequate hydroelectric power in sufficient quantity and at reasonable rates, and on the other the lack of quick and modern means of communication with the larger centres of the province and of the rest of the country.
Quebec Hydro is at present completing a gigantic project which, through underwater cables laid on the bed of the St. Lawrence river from the north to the south shore, opposite Matane county, will extend the benefit of electric power to the mines of Gaspe and the whole of the peninsula.
By virtue of this bill, which will increase to $2 million the capital stock of the Bonaventure and Gaspe Telephone Company, that company will be able to carry out a program of development and modernization of its telephone system, a program which calls for the investment of more than $1 million during the coming years.
For the last ten years or so the Gaspe peninsula has been undergoing a complete change in its fisheries and its agriculture along with its commercial and industrial expansion.
Seaports, wharves and fishing harbours have been built at great cost on the north side as well as on the south side of the peninsula. New shipyards, including that of Gaspe, are modernizing fishing fleets and changing the age-long Gaspe fishing industry. One of the largest plants for the production of fish by-products has just been built in Paspebiac, in Bonaventure county.
Private Bills
In recent years a federal experimental farm for the farming people of this important district of the province was also established in Bonaventure county.
Improvements to the Matapedia-Gaspe railroad branch line have certainly been noteworthy and continuous.
A belt highway, fully paved on practically its whole length, runs around the peninsula. Good roads, allowing both summer and winter [DOT] traffic between the counties of Gaspe North, Gaspe South and Bonaventure, were built inland, and connect Mont Louis and St. Anne des Monts with Murdochville, Gaspe and Cascapedia.
It is now the turn of the telephone network of the Gaspe peninsula to undergo the transformations and modernization which have been expected for so many years.
On many occasions in the past, and especially on March 13, 1952, I drew the attention of the house to the urgency of carrying out the improvements of the telephone network which serves both the Bonaventure and Gaspe constituencies.
I am therefore pleased to introduce this bill providing for an increase of the share capital of the Bonaventure and Gaspe Telephone Company to $2 million, allowing this company to go ahead with a development program, to face the increasing demand for better equipment, and to improve and extend its services.
The telephone network modernization program will cost the company more than a million dollars, of which almost half a million will immediately be invested in the installation of new equipment in the following localities: Oak Bay, Carleton, New Richmond, St. Alphonse, Caplan, Bonaventure, New Carlisle, Paspebiac and Port Daniel, in the county of Bonaventure, and Chandler, Grande Riviere, Cap d'Espoir, Perce, Barachois, Gaspe, Riviere au Renard and Cap des Rosiers, in the county of Gaspe. In these communities the company will multiply its lines so as to decrease to a considerable extent the number of party-line subscribers.
This company already has on file close to 600 applications for new telephones, both business or private, in the counties of Bonaventure and Gaspe. At present the company cannot act on those applications because of the heavy load its lines are carrying at this time. The Bonaventure and Gaspe Telephone Company Limited proposes to instal 3,000 new telephones on its lines between now and 1957. For all those reasons, I believe that the house should not hesitate to grant the powers requested in this bill.

He said: As I indicated on first reading, the purpose of this bill is to have the political affiliations of the various candidates placed on the ballots. From time to time in elections there are candidates with similar names on the ballot papers, which causes a great deal of confusion amongst the electors. For example, in the general election of 1953 there were six ridings where at least two candidates had the same name. In one riding there were two candidates named Langlois and one named Langlais; in another riding, two named Poulin; in another riding, two named Robi-chaud; in another riding, two named Cassel-man; and in another two named Meunier. This illustration takes into account only those
Canada Elections Act
cases where the names are identical. In many cases names are similar phonetically or in some other way, and a great deal of confusion arises from this situation. Electors might have considerable difficulty in determining which candidate belongs to which party.
Probably more serious is the fact that quite frequently at nominating conventions I am sure the best man is not nominated because his name is similar to that of a candidate running for another party. An example of that exists right now in the constituency of Battle River-Camrose, where a by-election is pending and where there are two candidates named Smith running for office. I am convinced this will cause a great deal of confusion to the electors in that riding. Three of the provinces in Canada have already adopted this legislation and are finding it most effective.

I have heard many expressions of satisfaction concerning the fact that in our provincial elections in British Columbia, as has already been mentioned, reference is made on the ballot papers to the political affiliation of the various candidates. My observation is that people in my area, generally speaking, feel it is a sensible thing in the age in which we are now living.
I have heard a great many expressions of dissatisfaction, particularly at the time of a federal election, concerning the fact that there is no similar provision in the federal elections act. I can recall discussions which took place in British Columbia at the time this particular arrangement was introduced, to the effect that in some way it contravened the constitutional theory upon which our parliamentary institutions are based; but certainly its introduction into the British Columbia election act has not had a shattering effect upon our parliamentary institutions in that province as far as I can see. Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words against the bill. I must admit I do not feel very strongly one way or the other, but I think I have too strong a streak of Scottish ancestry in me to want to spend money unless I can see that the spending of the money is going to achieve some good result for the country.
Frankly I cannot see that the results in the provincial elections in British Columbia, Alberta or Saskatchewan were any more intelligent than the result in the last federal election, held immediately following those provincial elections. We got that result in the federal election without having the ballot papers made a yard long with all these unnecessary names of political parties, and I for one believe that the onus is certainly on those who want a change made by adding the names of the parties.
The hon. member who introduced the bill pointed out that you can have Smith versus Smith. We will say there is a case where there is a Smith who is a Social Crediter, a Smith who is a C.C.F.'er and a Smith who is a Liberal. I must say that if the voters of any constituency are not intelligent enough to find out which Smith belongs to which party it is a sad commentary on the level of intelligence in that particular political party.
I am well aware that over the years there have been some very smart tricks played politically. I can remember hearing about the father of a former premier of Ontario, Hon. G. Howard Ferguson. Back in the days of John A. Macdonald he had great difficulty in retaining the official Conservative party nomination, but he emerged victor in one dominion election by the simple expedient of having tacked on a tree outside each polling station in the riding of Grenville, I believe it was, a short letter reading, "I commend my friend, Mr. Ferguson, to the support of the electors", and signed "John A. Macdonald". Of course there was quite a ruckus after the election, because the next day it turned out that the John A. Macdonald 
who had signed the letter was not the famous Sir John A. Macdonald, the prime minister, but John A. Macdonald the blacksmith in the home town of Mr. Ferguson's father.
I submit to hon. members that the change now suggested would make for no improvement over what we now have. If it is true that you can have confusion in the names of candidates, it is also true that you can have confusion in the names of parties. I have heard it said that there would never have been a Social Credit government in British Columbia if a great number of the voters had not been confused by "Social Credit" and "socialist". We have had one speaker each from the Social Credit and C.C.F. parties support this proposal, but we who sit in the house know very well that these parties are poles apart. Yet it is a fact that their own supporters in the province of British Columbia gave the other party second choice votes because it was not sufficiently clear in their own minds that Social Crediters were very different from C.C.F.'ers. Therefore I submit that this proposal would simply mean an unnecessary cluttering of the ballot and an unnecessary expense, and I for one propose to vote against it.

Let me point out to the hon. member for Vancouver South that the bill proposes to make at least one of these tricks impossible in the future. That is why it is introduced. Let me point out how very confusing it is to present to the people of a constituency the names of two candidates that are the same and ask the people to vote on them. Our federal constituencies are very large. Most of them have upwards of 50,000 voters, with many of them coming close to 100,000. It is virtually impossible for any person, no matter what his name, to become known definitely to all these voters. In the main the voters have to depend for some lead to the identity of a candidate on the ballot itself.
Let us take the present situation in Battle River-Camrose, referred to by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin. Here you have two candidates by the name of Smith, a very common name. I am not going to suggest that the Liberals, who held their nominating convention after the Social Crediters had held theirs, deliberately selected a man by the name of Smith in order to confuse the people of that constituency. I would not lay a charge of that kind. But the fact is that after the Social Crediters had nominated their candidate they did select a man by the name of Smith, and they knew full well at the time that there would be no indication whatsoever on the ballot as to the political affiliation of the Smith they nominated.
I point out this quite obvious fact. I shall make mine very brief so the government whip will have time to make his.
The reference in the bill is to the name of the political party or interest represented by the candidate. I want to raise two questions there. "Or interest"; what does that mean? Does that mean lawyers or doctors or undertakers or anybody you like? What does it mean? Second, suppose on the eve of an election a couple of friends decide to form a new party. Let us call it the populist party or the XYZ party, anything you like. Suppose I were a candidate, and suppose the hon. member for Hastings-Frontenac (Mr. White) were the president. We form the party just before the election-find any grand name for it you like-and as I understand it, provided I get a certificate from my friend that
[Mr. Byrne.)
I am the recognized candidate of our party I may have myself put down as such on the ballot.
How many of these are there to be? Seriously speaking, it seems to me to verge on the fantastic. There is no definition of a political party; it merely says "political party or interest". What does that mean? I suggest this provision has not been very carefully thought through, and altogether it would appear as though it would create confusion. I cannot see how the electoral officer can be guided, because the situation I put forward is not a fantastic one. There may be only four parties now, but we might run into an election with 14 parties, and the electoral officer would have to carry out the directions of this provision. I do not know whether or not he would have any discretion but it seems to me that if anyone wanted to put up a joke, if anyone wanted to organize a party just before an election and make the whole thing foolish, this would open the door wide for him to do so. I am afraid I am going to have to ask to be allowed to vote against it.

I only want to say a word or two following the line of thought expressed by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell). There is one other possible development that might be difficult to take care of under this bill, and that is if a man changed his affiliation on the eve of an election. Suppose he ran under another banner; where would he be? My hon. friends of the Social Credit group, if they continue, might find that in some constituencies they have more than one candidate all trying to run under the Social Credit banner. Have they considered how they are going to differentiate between them?
I think the real point in this matter is that we are not elected here as parties, we are elected as individuals. The party is only used as the machinery for the election. The party is only used as an instrument for the election, and we are here as individuals. I do not see why the elections act should be changed to say that we are elected as party people.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE POLITICAL AFFILIATION OF CANDIDATES ON BALLOT PAPERS
speechtext:
In view of the objections that have been raised to the bill, I think we could judge the effectiveness of this measure by the experience in parts of Canada that have legislation of this type. All of the objections that have been raised by previous speakers, and particularly the last two speakers, have not been borne out by experience in Saskatchewan. I think it is utterly ridiculous to suggest that all these imaginary faults will arise. We have conducted elections in Saskatchewan where the

name of the candidate and that of his party-have been on the ballot, and I do not think that form of ballot has in any way complicated the holding of the elections. I do not believe confusion has arisen in any circumstances from putting party labels on ballots; and I can recall several instances where, before party labels were placed on ballots, we did run into difficulties of that kind. For instance, mention has been made of two persons having similar names.
So I suggest in all seriousness that the objections raised against the bill are not sound. In some parts of Canada we have had this type of ballot, and nothing in their experience has indicated that the bill now before the house would bring about the difficulties envisaged by those opposing it.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE POLITICAL AFFILIATION OF CANDIDATES ON BALLOT PAPERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the risk of arousing the derisive laughter of my friends in the corner I think I should take the traditionalist view of this, and repeat what has been said by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), that nowhere in our federal elections act is there any mention of any political party. In our experience in the past in trying to draft the elections act we have always carefully avoided mentioning political parties, and for the reason-you may laugh at it-that whatever we may do in practice, members of parliament are sent here to give our constituents the benefit of the best of our judgment and the best of our ability to determine what should be done in the interests of the country as a whole.
Except perhaps during the time when we were occupying the hustings, for many years we have done our best to say that we are non-partisan in our outlook on matters coming before us. It seems almost an insult to tell a man he is a politician. Now, under the guise of a great reform, we are asked to label ourselves as politicians. We will come here and, in the words of some statesman of long ago, we will be all for the party and none for the state.
It seems to me we have not reached the stage in this country where we are going to set up throughout the country political machines and political organizations to which members will become so attached that it will be very difficult for them to take an impartial and non-partisan view of matters coming before the house. If on the ballot paper itself an individual who proposes to become a member of parliament labelled himself, for the time during which he will be a member, as the supporter of such and such a party, it would be extremely difficult for him, both in conscience and in the view of his electors, to say that from now on he repudiates the
Canada Elections Act
pledge he made to his electors when he said he was a Liberal, a Conservative, a Social Crediter, or anything else you may mention.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE POLITICAL AFFILIATION OF CANDIDATES ON BALLOT PAPERS
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? Would he apply the same argument to the literature put out by candidates during an election campaign?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE POLITICAL AFFILIATION OF CANDIDATES ON BALLOT PAPERS
speechtext:
Quite right; but none of that literature is official, other than being official in the sense of the party. It is not sanctioned by the parliament of Canada, nor by the people of Canada represented in the house by their members.
Up to the present time we have religiously avoided what is suggested in this bill. I remember the trouble we had in framing the elections act in order to have enumerators from two political parties making up the lists. We had to find such language as "a representative of an opposite and adverse political party" if I remember correctly. During the first overseas election-I am not speaking of the one in 1917, but the one in 1940

we refrained from stating the political allegiance of the persons who were candidates. I admit frankly that we received innumerable complaints on that score. But in 1945, if I recall correctly, there was some kind of arrangement made whereby political parties were not recognized but leaders of groups in the house were given recognition. It was stated either on the ballot or in the literature-I think perhaps it was in the literature sent out by the returning officer-that such and such a candidate was endorsed by the leader of the opposition or by the leader of the government, or something of that nature. But I doubt if the word "Liberal" or the word "Conservative" or "C.C.F." was on the ballot, though, in saying this, of course, I am speaking only from memory.
Besides, I doubt if we can here, by legislation, give to the leader of the government, for those of us sitting on this side of the house a copyright on the name "Liberal". I have as much right to call myself a Liberal, even though I might oppose some of the policies of the right hon. gentleman who leads us. In the same way, hon. gentlemen sitting in the opposition can call themselves Progressive Conservatives and still not ask for the endorsation of the hon. gentleman sitting opposite.
Under the circumstances, then, I do not oppose this because it is an innovation, but rather because, in conformity with the customs, the habits and the traditions of our parliamentary institutions, I would strenuously oppose placing on the ballot paper the name of the political party to which a candidate adhered.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to take part in this debate not because of any specialized knowledge of grain production or grain handling, but solely to register a protest against what I consider to be unwarranted charges against several individuals of whom I happen to have personal knowledge.
The hon. member for Assiniboia has levelled a charge of incompetence, inefficiency and perhaps worse against two gentlemen for whom I have a very high regard. The chairman of the board of grain commissioners is a man of outstanding reputation in the province of Manitoba. As was said this afternoon, he is a man who has a long history of service to the farmers of western Canada. He certainly is a man who should be supposed to know a great deal about the handling of grain, and as such I would regard him as an eminent person to discharge the duties of the chairman of the board of grain commissioners. It is true he is a Liberal, but this is perhaps just unfortunate, Mr. Chairman, and perhaps it is not a vital handicap to enabling him to discharge the duties incident to his position.
With regard to the second person who has been mentioned in the hon. member's criticism, namely Mr. Milner, a member of the board, I also have personal knowledge of him. I know he has spent practically a lifetime in the grain business. It amuses me somewhat to hear the proposal to pay Mr. Milner a salary of $14,000 per annum questioned, because I know that over a period of years he has probably commanded three times or four times that amount in the private grain trade. Those companies paid him this amount of money for no other reason than they expected him to make money for them. This is to me certainly an indication that Mr. Milner is eminently qualified for his job.
I would think that on reflection the hon. member for Assiniboia might possibly change his conception in this regard. Perhaps his attitude to date indicates, let us say, a certain measure of immaturity of judgment.

This resolution was debated at some length yesterday by the hon. member for Eglinton. Had the program of business been such that I had followed him yesterday, I would have spoken at greater length than I will do now. However, I would like to say a few words with regard to the point of view he expressed yesterday.
It is true that the bill to be based on this resolution is more far-reaching than might be thought from the brevity of the resolution and the bill itself. That fact arises, of course,

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
from the intention to wipe out the expiry date, which has the effect of making the Department of Defence Production as permanent as any other department of the government.
However, I do not share all the alarms expressed yesterday by the hon. member for Eglinton, nor do I go along with him in likening the act being amended by this resolution to the Emergency Powers Act or to the War Measures Act. It seems to me if there is going to be defence purchasing and defence procurement on a scale of any magnitude it is necessary for the government to have powers to protect the economy of the country against the inflationary effects of those purchases and procurements.
When this legislation was brought in in 1951 we felt those powers were necessary. Indeed, if we have any quarrel with the minister or the government regarding the powers contained in this legislation it is because of the fact they have not used the powers that are in the bill to prevent the cost of living from climbing to the extent it has. I think there is no question about the inflationary effect of defence procurements, purchases and building. In my view the cost of housing, which is higher today than a few years ago, is a direct result of expenditures by the government under the heading of defence. That being the case, it seems necessary that there be powers to control the economy. Certainly there is a wide difference between this legislation and the Emergency Powers Act. That act was wide and undefined. As far as this legislation is concerned, at least we know what it contains.
Nevertheless, as the hon. member for Eglinton said yesterday, it is true that before passing the bill it will be well for us to look at the Defence Production Act which is now on the statute books and realize what it is that we are re-enacting. Naturally we will do that before we come to the second reading of the bill itself.
I have one further comment to make in connection with this proposed legislation. As the Minister of Trade and Commerce will recall, I drew attention to the fact last year, when the Salaries Act was being amended, that there was no provision in that act for the salary of the Minister of Defence Production. Neither he nor I worried much about that omission because, as he put it on page 2323 of Hansard of February 23, 1954: However, if the salary were to be increased the act would have to be amended, or an item would be put in the estimates for that purpose. Frankly I think it is just on oversight. I think the salary in question might just as well have been listed here, but it is not listed and I am not going to ask for an amendment. Somehow or other I hope to get my salary.
Defence Production Act
We all know he gets his salary as the Minister of Trade and Commerce so this is merely an academic matter. Therefore the amount really is not in issue, but it seems to me it should be put in the same statute that provides for the salaries of the other cabinet ministers. That provision is made in chapter 21 of the statutes of 1953-54, which sets out the salaries of all the other ministers of the crown and also the salary of the Solicitor General, even though his position is in a slightly different category. It seems to me a bit untidy to have all the other salaries provided for in one place and the salary of the Minister of Defence Production specified in the act which provides for the department itself.
I suggest seriously, for the purpose of keeping these things tidy and having them where they can be readily found, that before the bill is brought in consideration might be given to taking the provision for the salary of the Minister of Defence Production out of the Defence Production Act and putting it in the Salaries Act, along with the salaries of the other cabinet ministers.

Mr. Chairman, as the hon. member for Eglinton indicated yesterday, the official opposition are not opposing the salary increase for the Minister of Defence Production or the proposal to make the department permanent, but we do believe that before this is done there should be a thorough review of the powers granted by the Defence Production Act. When the defence production bill was under debate in 1951 second reading was moved by the Prime Minister, but the Minister of Trade and Commerce made the speech and he had this to say about the bill, as found at page 836 of Hansard of March 2:
It is proposed that the act would expire on July 31, 1956. There is no particular significance to this date, other than to recognize-
These are the words I wish to emphasize, -that some of the powers sought in this bill are special powers which should not be of a continuing nature.
That was the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce on March 2, 1951, four years ago. He himself said at that time that the Defence Production Act as introduced, and as it stands today, contained special powers which should not be of a continuing nature. We adopt the argument of the Minister of Trade and Commerce on the introduction of this very same legislation four years ago, namely that there are some powers in the act which should not be of a continuing nature. We suggest with the utmost sincerity that a look should be taken at these powers in the Defence Production Act, which the Minister of Trade and Commerce himself

Defence Production Act thought should not be of a continuing nature, because of course the proposal now is that all the powers in the act are to be made permanent in that the section giving the department a life of only a period of years is to be repealed by the bill which is to follow the resolution.
The hon. member for Eglinton yesterday listed different powers in the Defence Production Act which he thought should not be made permanent. I do not intend to go over all of them again this evening, but I do wish to point out three or four which it seems to me it is very unwise and unnecessary to place in any measure providing for the powers of a permanent department.
First of all, under section 23 of the Defence Production Act power is given to the minister -not to the cabinet but to the minister-to make a person undertake a contract. If they refuse the minister can compel them to contract. One of the penalties for refusing is that the minister can, under section 27, appoint a controller to take over the business, not only take over the part of the business producing the article he requires but their whole business, even though only a small part of it may have to do with the production of the article required by the minister. Under the act this power can be exercised not only by the minister but by his appointee. These are terrifically wide powers. Section 23 reads in part as follows:
Where a person who has been requested to enter into a defence contract on terms and conditions that the minister considers to be fair and reasonable has refused or failed to enter into the contract, if the minister is satisfied that such person owns or controls facilities that are suitable for or can be adapted to the work required to carry out such contract and that his refusal or failure was without reasonable excuse, the minister may direct that person to produce, deliver or store, or to construct, as the case may be, on such terms and conditions and within such period as the minister considers to be fair and reasonable in the circumstances, the defence supplies or the defence project or projects that would have been the subject matter of the contract if it had been entered into.
That gives the minister or his appointee the widest possible power. Section 27 contains the power to put a controller in charge of the business. In one case it can be done where a man has refused to contract. Perhaps I had better read the section so that memories will be refreshed as to how far it goes. It reads as follows:
Where the minister is satisfied that
(a) a person who has entered into a defence contract has failed or is likely to fail to perform the contract in a businesslike and efficient manner . . .
(c) a person to whom a direction has been given under section 23-
That is the section I just read.
-or who is required pursuant to a regulation to give priority in the carrying on of his business to

the production of or dealing in defence supplies, or construction of defence projects has failed without reasonable excuse to comply with the direction or regulation or-
Here is another amazing power.
-the minister is satisfied that he will so fail or is likely so to fail, the minister may authorize another person, in this act called a "controller", to carry on, until the minister otherwise directs, the whole or any part of the business of that person.
The controller the minister puts in charge of the business is given the widest powers by the following subsection:
(2) Where a controller has been appointed to carry on a business or a part thereof, he shall be deemed to be the agent of the owner thereof for the purpose of carrying on the business or that part thereof, except that the owner shall not have any right to control the business or that part thereof and the controller may, subject to any instructions of the minister, do all such things as he thinks fit for the purpose of carrying on the business or that part thereof.
There is no freedom left to business in Canada, Mr. Chairman, so long as that particular provision remains on the statute books of our land. Then there is a further power in section 29 to inquire into a person's business. The section reads:
29. (1) The minister may, whenever he deems it expedient, cause an inquiry to be made into and concerning any matter relating to or incidental to or arising out of a defence contract or any group or series of defence contracts or any dealings in or with defence supplies, and may appoint a person or persons by whom the inquiry shall be conducted.
A later subsection provides that an investigator appointed by the minister may or may not allow any person whose conduct is being investigated to have a lawyer. The subsection goes just that far. In these provisions we have a potential tyranny in our land.
There is a further provision in section 28 concerning the cabinet. All the other powers I have cited can be exercised by the minister alone, but this section 28 reads:
The governor in council may, by order, direct that a person shall not be bound by any obligation, restriction or limitation imposed on that person by or under any statute, order, rule, regulation, by-law, or contract with respect to such matters as may be specified in the order affecting the entry into or performance of a defence contract by that person or the carrying out of an order made by the minister under this act.
This means, Mr. Chairman, that the cabinet can override a statute of this parliament, a statute of any provincial parliament or a bylaw of any municipality if they see fit. They can say to a businessman, "Here, you need not comply with any of these other laws or bylaws; you have to do what we say, or else." If the businessman does not comply he may become subject to the heavy penalties contained in this act.
When this Defence Production Act was being discussed in 1951 we complained about

the drastic powers. We pointed out that those powers were identical to powers taken by the government in wartime. These are not peacetime powers, these are full wartime powers which the government took in 1951 and is now trying to put on the statute books of Canada in a permanent measure. In the debate which took place in 1951 I questioned the Prime Minister on that point. I am reading now from page 908 of Hansard for March 5, 1951:

Then, may I ask the Prime Minister whether any further powers would be required to carry out defence production if we were actually in a third world war?
Here is the answer:

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not anticipate there would be. I think the enabling sections here are expressed in language which probably would be broad enough to apply; but of course, with respect to that, as with respect to all our other moves in this connection, we would expect to declare any change in policy to parliament, and we would have to be asking parliament to appropriate moneys, so there would be ample opportunity for parliament to concur or refuse to concur in the carrying out of any further policy that was declared.

The Prime Minister has said that
this bill as presented contains all the powers that would be required in the event of a third world war.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I would not want to promise
the house that if we ran up against something where the courts said this was not good enough we would not come back to parliament; if we thought it should be done, we would ask parliament to authorize it-
Here are the significant words in the Prime Minister's statement:
-but I think the law officers have drawn this in language that should be sufficient to cover all the enabling powers apt to be required.
There is an admission by the Prime Minister that the Defence Production Act contains all the powers that the government could foresee being required if we were in a third world war. The bill which is to follow this resolution makes those powers part of the permanent law of this country.
I refer also to the Department of Defence Production report for the period from April 1 to December 31, 1951. This was the first report after the department was set up. I find this at page 14:
Although the powers now in effect are virtually the same as those which existed during the last war, it has been understood that these powers would be used to the minimum extent necessary.
There the department itself also recognizes, as the Prime Minister had previously recognized, that the Defence Production Act contains the full wartime powers.
About a year ago the Prime Minister was faced with the question of whether the Emergency Powers Act would be continued in effect. This act, of course, was a twin to the
Defence Production Act Defence Production Act. We were complaining about both these statutes. The Emergency Powers Act had to be renewed last year, otherwise it was going to expire. The Prime Minister finally decided that it should expire, and this is what he said when he made his statement to the house, as recorded at page 4229 of Hansard for April 29, 1954:
However, I can assure my hon. friend at the present time we have come to the conclusion we will not at this session ask parliament to extend the Emergency Powers Act. We felt it was a grave decision to make because there is still a pretty explosive situation existing in the world. I hope the situation will not require the exercise of any but normal powers by the governor in council. But should it develop that there would have to be, in the interests of the safety of the nation, powers exercised that are not normally conferred upon the governor in council by existing legislation, we would have to resort to the War Measures Act.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, there is just as much reason for getting the Defence Production Act on a proper basis, under which there will be no greater powers than those that should be granted by the parliament of a free nation which is not at war. If the nation were at war, or if there were apprehended war, there is, as we all know, power in the cabinet to bring into effect the War Measures Act, under which the government would have all the power it could possibly need.
In introducing this resolution yesterday, the Prime Minister pointed out, at page 1904, that the peak of the defence program was past. We are now in the position where, on the authority of the Prime Minister himself, we can say the peak of the defence production has passed. He went on to say that the government kept these powers because of certain things, and he mentioned aircraft production, the production of electronics and some other war goods of that type. I do not believe anyone in the house would object to the government taking very wide powers in connection with the production of aircraft, for example, or munitions of war. No one wants to handicap the defence department in its work of keeping the defences of this country strong.
The difficulty is that the Defence Production Act does not define defence supplies as consisting only of aircraft, electronics, ships and munitions of war. The act defines defence supplies in such a broad way that they include everything. They include underwear for the troops; carpets for barracks and every other conceivable thing. I refer to the definition of "defence supplies" contained in section 2 (f). It reads:
"Defence supplies" means:
(i)	arms, ammunition, implements of war, Vehicles, mechanical and other equipment, watercraft, amphibious craft, aircraft, animals-

Defence Production Act
There is no restriction on "animals". I suppose it includes everything from cooties to elephants.
-articles, material, substances and things required or used lor the purposes ol the defence of Canada or lor co-operative efforts for defence being carried on by Canada and an associated government.
(ii)	ships of all kinds-
Not only warships, but "ships of all kinds".
(iii)	articles, materials, substances-
This, by the way, is the clause which gives the all-embracing powers:
(iil) articles, materials, substances and things of all kinds used for the production or supply of anything mentioned in subparagraph (i) or (ii) or for the construction of defence projects.
That, in effect, covers the whole of Canada's productive capacity. Practically anything produced in Canada can be placed by the minister in the category of a defence supply. We suggest that one way to get out of the difficulty would be for the government to revise the definition of "defence supplies", and put in only the things over which it needs these drastic controls.
There is no excuse in the world for assuming this all-embracing power over practically everything that Canadians can produce. Parliament in a free country should not be asked to give these powers to any department of government on a permanent basis. Yet that is what we are going to be asked to do in the bill which will follow this resolution. Once these powers go on the statute books in permanent form they will never come off. The authority will be there for all time. It will be there a long time after the present Minister of Defence Production is out of the picture.
Some people might say, "Oh well, give him the power; let him have whatever power he wants." But this question goes far beyond any one man. This power is going to be on the statute books, available to whoever may be the minister of defence production a year from now, five years from now or ten years from now. It is a dangerous precedent to establish, in giving power to any department of government.
Where does Canadian business stand as long as there is a law of this kind on the statute books? Every business in this nation is under the thumb of the Department of Defence Production by reason of these powers. They are all under the threat of that department. Whether or not those threats are ever used, there is the power in the department to threaten every business in Canada.
The Minister of Defence Production has made his attitude very clear on legislation of this kind. I was questioning him in 1950,
tMr. Green.1
at which time we were considering a bill which became the Essential Materials (Defence) Act. Here is what he said on September 8, 1950, as reported at page 460 of Hansard-and this was the present Minister of Defence Production speaking at that time-
I suggest to the committee that a word from the government is more effective if there is a law in the background that can be applied in case the response is not all that may be desired.
Is Canada, is Canadian business, to be subject to possible dictatorship of this type? There was the attitude taken by the minister in 1950. Here are the powers taken in 1951, when the minister himself-this same minister-said that the Defence Production Act contained some powers that should not be continuing powers. In 1951 the Prime Minister said these were wartime powers, and the minister's own department repeated that statement in its annual report of 1951. Now, today, we have the final pay-off, when the government asks that these powers be made permanent.
Mr. Chairman, the appetite for arbitrary powers is still with those on the government's front benches. The war has been over for ten years, but the appetite for those arbitrary powers is still there, or the government would not be asking for the passage of this measure at the present session. Yesterday in my judgment the Prime Minister took the situation very lightly; he did not seem to be worrying much. He said, "Oh, well, we have to have aircraft produced, and we just want to carry on with these powers". There was no mention about the story of four years ago, that they were only going to be temporary. Now the Prime Minister is coming in and asking to have these powers made permanent.
I merely repeat the suggestion I made in opening this evening, and it is this; that before the measure is put through the government should review the powers contained in the Defence Production Act. Just let parliament have a look at these powers and decide which of them should be given to the Department of Defence Production. In addition, let the government take another look at the definition of "defence supplies". The Department of Defence Production should not be given on a permanent basis the powers it was given in 1951. We are urging the Prime Minister and the government sincerely and seriously to take another look at this measure before having it enacted into law.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the present act was put on the statute books in 1951. This is 1955. I must say that so far as defence production is concerned I find it difficult to distinguish between the situation in 1951 and the situation in 1955.

In 1951 we were starting a $5 billion defence program. I think something like $4,500 million has been spent on that program, and the work of the department is not in any way diminishing. I think we have today some of the most difficult projects in hand that it has ever been the responsibility of the department to undertake since it was formed.
I quite agree that all the powers set out in the act should not be continuing powers; but I do maintain that if they were necessary in 1951, they are just as necessary today. My hon. friend reads out these paragraphs as though they were fantastic.
They are.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Well, I can tell him that every one of those powers has been exercised during the period I have been in charge of defence production in this country, and exercised not once but many times. The reason they were put in the act is that experience during the second world war indicated that that type of power is necessary to mobilize the industry of this country for war.
May I ask a question? Has the minister used those powers within the last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
No; they have not been needed. Another thing, with respect to the alarm that my hon. friend expressed about the position of industry, that has never been suggested by industry. I know of no one who does not take defence contracts, all the defence contracts they can get under this act; they are very glad to do so, and I have yet to have any complaints from industry that the powers of the act are unusually broad.
As the Prime Minister has pointed out, there is a continuing need for a department to carry out the procurement functions of the Canadian defence program. The requirements of the Department of National Defence for the foreseeable future are of sizeable proportions. The people of Canada expect the armed forces to be ready at a moment's notice to perform their duties in the defence of this country and to fulfil our international commitments. I feel that the Department of Defence Production must be so constituted that it can perform its functions with similar dispatch. I feel it does not make sense from any point of view to have a strong military force without the backing of an equally strong procurement agency, properly equipped to do its job.
The hon. member for Eglinton has implied that because there have been no adverse repercussions from the revoking of the Emergency Powers Act, there would be none if
Defence Production Act the Defence Production Act were changed. This is not true. The two acts are not the same, and the powers of the Emergency Powers Act were much wider than those of the Defence Production Act.
Not only is the authority of the Defence Production Act needed to enable the department to act quickly in an emergency, but it is needed to carry out the continuing functions of the department in line with our present defence commitments. We are just embarking on the construction of the mid-Canada early warning line, which is the largest project of this kind we have ever undertaken. On the aircraft side a number of major production contracts, such as the Britannia, have just started and will not be completed for some time. New developments in the field of modern weapons, for example guided missiles, will place heavy responsibilities on the department in the years ahead. Furthermore, the need to maintain and keep up to date our present defence potential will require a high level of defence procurement. In other words there is every indication that the volume of defence orders will continue to be sufficiently large to warrant the continuation of the Department of Defence Production on a non-temporary basis, and with full authority to operate effectively.
There is no need for me to repeat the remarks of the Prime Minister on the need for a more permanent basis for the department in order to attract and retain the type of person needed to carry out the very responsible procurement functions of the future. I would, however, like to say something of the way in which the procurement functions have been carried out, and the use that has been made of the powers embodied in the Defence Production Act.
The best example is the way in which the control of essential materials was handled. As you will recall, in the early stages of the present defence program, some measure of control was needed to ensure adequate raw materials, primarily for the defence efforts of our allies. These, however, were kept to a minimum, and once the world supply situation improved all controls were removed, and at the present time there are no orders in effect. On the priorities side, assistance is given to Canadian defence contractors to participate in the limited priorities system that is still in operation in the United States.
However, the supply situation can change very rapidly, particularly for certain strategic materials which are not produced in sufficient quantities to meet large-scale defence requirements. It is, therefore, important that the authority to introduce control measures should be readily available.

Just to show how quickly that can change, I have a report that just arrived from Washington headed "Daily Report for Executives". It points out that nickel, copper and aluminum are all in short supply, and it discusses the need for putting these metals under control. We also received an announcement from Washington of the likelihood of stopping the export of scrap iron to Canada. A large part of Canada's scrap iron has always been imported from the United States, and if that move materializes we can have a very tight market in scrap iron, to the extent that it might seriously cripple our production of finished steel. These situations in times such as these are always possibilities; in fact they are more than possibilities, so why in the world should we strip ourselves of the powers to deal with those situations as they affect the national defence program of Canada?
The hon. member for Eglinton has questioned those sections of the act dealing with the control of essential materials and has implied that Canadian industry generally is apprehensive over the continuation of these powers. In actual fact the situation is just the reverse. The first request for the introduction of controls comes from industry. Even today I am under considerable pressure from Canadian manufacturers to recommend to the governor in council the re-establishment of certain control measures.
In order to carry out procurement functions properly the department must have certain powers, regardless of whether it is a temporary or a permanent department and regardless of whether it is dealing with an emergency situation or a continuing defence program. Among these powers is that of renegotiation. I am sure all hon. members will agree that there must be control over costs and profits on defence contracts. Experience after the last war on the renegotiation of contracts was invaluable in setting up our present policy and procedures. The very existence of the renegotiation section has, I feel, contributed to keeping the record very satisfactory, and so far there has been no need to invoke this section of the act. However, the need for such authority still remains and will continue as long as we are dealing with defence orders of the present magnitude, such as are represented by the major aircraft and electronic contracts to which I have referred.
In discussing the question of the need for a properly constituted department to carry out procurement functions, I would point out that we have had an opportunity to gain a good deal of experience in how this should be handled. We have gone from the department of munitions and supply, through the


department of reconstruction and supply, to the period when procurement was handled by a crown company, Canadian Commercial Corporation, and back again to a department. There is no doubt in my mind that the Defence Production Act provides for the type of department that is required for Canada's defence program.
Another power under the act I would like to mention is that dealing with assistance in setting up defence production facilities. The need to establish new crown-owned facilities to increase our industrial defence potential has, for the most part, been met. The provision of such plant and equipment has decreased to the point where only $14 million was spent last year out of a total of $172 million since the department was established, and this was largely for projects approved in previous years. Encouragement has been given to private investment, through accelerated depreciation, to set up facilities having little or no value to normal commercial operations and where the probable production period enables the assets to be substantially written off.
Here, too, the picture is one of decreasing use of this policy as the need for special facilities has declined. Nevertheless, as the defence program continues and as new developments lead to new fields of production, there will be cases in which the crown should carry the burden of investment as well as those in which industry should receive assistance through additional capital cost allowances.
Under section 17 (e) (i) of the act, the Minister of Defence Production has the authority to place contracts without prior approval of treasury board. I would like to point out that this authority has only been used to meet emergency situations, but we would be in an intolerable situation if there were not such a section in the act. Inevitably, in a large defence program, circumstances will arise which demand immediate action, and I am not prepared to admit that there is anything improper in retaining such authority.
At the present time use is being made of this authority in a few special cases to purchase materials required for the two early warning lines-mid-Canada and D.E.W. In the latter case, certain urgent requirements are purchased by the Department of National Defence through the Department of Defence Production, with reimbursement by the United States government.
In conclusion I would like to ask, where is this apprehension on the part of Canadian industry over the Defence Production Act? I am not aware of any such fears. In fact there is no indication of any reluctance on the part of industry to enter into contracts with

the department. Of course some people complain that they cannot make enough profit on defence contracts. Others complain because they are not getting enough defence business. But no complaints have been made to me that the powers of the act are too wide or that they hamper business operations.
In my opinion it is essential, in view of the kind of world in which we are now living, that we have a Department of Defence Production staffed with experienced and efficient personnel and with the powers to perform its operations on a continuing basis.

Mr. Chairman, it is one of the least popular and exciting occupations in the world to try to champion the rule of law. Law is such a dull thing that it is hard for us to believe that it is by the rule of law we live, and it is necessary that it should have vigilant guardians or one day we may wake up too late, to find we have lost it.
It was a great disappointment to me tonight to find during the course of this debate that this act is to be continued in its full powers by the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister is a great jurist, and I would have hoped that he would have been zealous in carrying out the request, which seemed to me a reasonable one, made yesterday by the hon. member for Eglinton. However, I gether from the demeanour of the Prime Minister and from what the Minister of Defence Production has said that that is not going to be done. The hon. member for Eglinton said, as reported on page 1909 of Hansard of March 10:
The course the government ought to follow now in my submission, Mr. Chairman, is to revise the bill they propose to introduce following this resolution, and to substitute a bill which will reconfer only those powers that are really necessary to the continuation of the defence program under existing circumstances.
The Minister of Defence Production made a great point tonight of the fact that things are working very smoothly. I believe that; I am glad to think that, and that is one reason, as I shall argue later, why we do not need these extraordinary powers. The minister says there is no difference between 1951 and 1955, but I submit that there is a great difference. There has been an interval of four years; there have been four years of practice with the business interests of this country. The minister has said that he receives no complaints from the business interests. I can believe that; I am not going to argue that.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Have you received any complaints?

My argument is that it is the duty of people like ourselves, indeed that
Defence Production Act we are sent here for that purpose, to try to reflect on the basic conditions under which we live. We ought to be the champions of law. I know it is so much nicer to have power, and I expect that if I were in the minister's position I would want power too. Perhaps it is only because I am a humble member of the opposition and not distracted by the many duties the minister has that I consider myself so much wiser on this particular point than he.
We like to think in the opposition that we are practical men. We know the minister is doing a job, and I do not hesitate for a moment to say that he is doing it well. But we also say that anyone who will take time off to think about it can see how much easier it is for the minister to have these powers. The minister has told us quite frankly that it is nice to have power at his back, because then the people you are negotiating with will be much more reasonable, much more pliable and much more bendable to your will. If you cannot persuade them you can just stand back and crack them.
The minister has been frank about that, but I suggest that to leave arbitrary power on the statute books for that reason is a dangerous thing. We are bringing up a whole generation of young people to whom the abnormal quickly becomes the normal, and to whom these powers which stagger those of us who have been brought up under democratic laws are going to become commonplace. I was greatly disappointed to hear the Prime Minister say, as reported on page 1905 of Hansard:
In the present unsettled state of international affairs I do not feel that the time has come to take out of the act those powers which are there and which enable the department to deal expeditiously with any situation that would interfere with the regular maintenance of Canada's defensive strength and the regular carrying out of Canada's undertaking.
That is another way of saying that if this bill is passed and the Defence Production Act made permanent, or at any rate without a time limit, the abnormal will quickly become the normal. I quoted what the hon. member for Eglinton had to say. Of course the danger that faces us all is that in defending freedom we may be driven to take steps which are utterly inconsistent with what we are defending. I am going to take the liberty of quoting a humble authority who spoke on this four years ago by the name of Macdonnell, and I quote from page 865 of Hansard of March 2, 1951, as follows:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I was drawing its attention to some of the defects, as I thought, in the bill now before us. I had suggested that the powers given in the bill were virtually going to turn the business of the country into an economy living by the grace of one man.

Defence Production Act the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). I was wrong in one particular. I should not have said one man. I should have said one man and a host of delegates of that one man, which on the whole makes the thing much worse because can we believe that we are going to have a large number of men who have the qualities of experience, knowledge, wisdom, moderation and singlemindedness that are going to be necessary to exercise these far-reaching and virtually unlimited powers described to us this afternoon by. my leader?
Four years have passed, During those four years this department has been working, as the minister has pointed out to us, and we are glad to admit what he has said about the way it has worked. People have become accustomed to working with the department. While I am a cautious man I would hazard a small sum that if one asked the minister off the record if he really needed these powers to get on with his job and to have the businessmen of Canada work for him, he would give one of those smiles of his which suggest "What do you take me for?"
I do not believe he needs these full powers. In the first place I do not believe there is 1 per cent of the businessmen of Canada who are so unpatriotic that they would not be reasonable in carrying out what they are asked to do. In fact I understood the minister to say that over the last year they had not needed to invoke these powers. In any event I am bold enough to believe that the Minister of Defence Production is a forceful enough man to know how to deal with these people without all these arbitrary powers which practically clothe the minister with the same power that Stalin had during his lifetime. I am bold enough to believe we can get on without that. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra said, and it is no exaggeration, "When you read that act, ask yourself if there is any freedom left". You just cannot find it. They were good lawyers who drafted that act, and they did not leave many loopholes. I think the most fantastic thing was, if I can remember the wording and paraphrase it, "where the minister has reason to think that a company may not be able to carry out," these tremendous powers suddenly fall into his hands.
The proper course was that taken with respect to the Emergency Powers Act. We ran whatever risk there was to run. After all, we are not in the horse and buggy days, and it does not take three months to summon parliament; parliament can be summoned in 48 hours if necessary. I think the real reason, and perhaps the only reason, is that it is so much easier to come back with a little bill of two clauses, one of which says the salary of the minister is to be raised from $10,000 to $15,000 and the other cancels the section
[Mr. Macdonnell.1
which made the bill temporary. Of course it is easier to do that than to do what the hon. member for Eglinton asked, namely to fine-tooth comb the bill and come up with a bill containing only the necessary powers. It is an easy thing for the government to say, "Give us the power; we are fine fellows and we won't abuse it". I do not know much about history, but I think you could look at history and find many cases where power was obtained on that basis and afterwards the people bitterly rued what they had done.
Before I take my seat I want to recall what happened four years ago. We disliked that bill very much, and we said a great deal in criticism of it. Perhaps we were weak in not voting against it, but in any event our motive was good. Our feeling at that time was that an emergency had suddenly come upon us. We were caught unprepared to a considerable extent. There were arrears which had to be made up. There was a war actually going on and it was a hot war at that time, although it was a long way off. The minister says that he has not much more confidence in the stability of affairs today, and perhaps he said he has even less.
No sane man denies the dangers which exist today, and I submit that if the minister had come asking to have the act extended for a year it might have been a different thing, but we are asked to make it part of the law of the land. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra says, if it goes through now it will never be changed. Certainly not in the lifetime of any of us.
I therefore submit that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is wrong when he says the situation has not changed since four years ago. I think it has. Anyway, I describe it as I see it. He has people working with him. He says he found no one who does not want to contract, which I submit is further proof of what I say. He does not need this superlative power. The business community, as it is called, works with him. The government does not need this power any more than a cow needs two tails.
Anyone who has any real feeling for his position in this house knows that the one thing we must take care of is the rule of law. We in the opposition have made a most reasonable request of the government. How reasonable was the request made by the hon. member for Eglinton! Can anyone suggest it is not reasonable? It is so moderate it is really rather a record for my friend. I shall read it again:
The course the government ought to follow now in my submission, Mr. Chairman, is to revise the bill they propose to introduce following this resolution, and to substitute a bill which will

reconfirm only those powers that are really necessary to the continuation of the defence program under existing circumstances.
On the basis of what the minister has said tonight I think it is fair to say that it is perfectly clear these powers could be cut down to some extent. When you read them some of the powers appear almost fantastic. I am somewhat surprised that we allowed them to pass four years ago without fighting against them, despite the circumstances of those years. All we ask now is to have these powers revised in the light of conditions today. In my opinion no one in this house believes they cannot be cut down to some extent. The government has taken the easy course in this regard. Four years ago-
