Thank you, Mr. Chairman. What has been said by the hon. member for Eglinton, the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, the hon. member for Greenwood and other members who have spoken against this legislation leads me to say that there is absolutely no need for the legislation to be made permanent. As was pointed out, the minister himself said in 1951 that these powers should not be made permanent. I should like to know what justification he finds now for making them permanent. There is none whatsoever. As the hon. member for Greenwood has said, the desire for power is simply unbounded among the members of the Liberal government on the front benches. I think this is an unnecessary piece of legislation, and there is no need for it. This kind of thing tends to make our country more and more a one-party state. It gives far too much power to one party. It is an unnecessary piece of legislation and, in my opinion, should be withdrawn.

Mr. Chairman, I had not intended to speak on the resolution tonight, but after listening to the speech of my friend

Defence Production Act the hon. member for Greenwood, I felt I would not be acting as a responsible member of the house if I did not say something in support of the argument he advanced. I did not hear the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra because I had to leave the chamber for a few minutes, but I am sure I would subscribe also to everything he said.
I am not saying anything now by way of reflection on the minister who is piloting the resolution through the committee. I quite agree with what the hon. member for Greenwood said. We have great respect for the minister. He has carried out the most onerous duties in a way which reflects credit on himself and has tended toward the efficient operation of his department and the government generally.
I have no hesitation whatsoever in saying that, but I do say, also without hesitation, that the measure he is introducing tonight is unnecessary and not, in my opinion, in any way in the interests of the country or in the interests of the parliamentary system and democracy generally. What is the situation which confronts us? Probably peace as we have known it in the past is not going to be our lot within the lifetime of any hon. member sitting in this chamber. I hope I am wrong, but I think that is a fair assumption. We are faced either with the prospect of a real war, a so-called hot war, if you want to use the headline expression, or we are going to have a long period of armed preparation so we can be in a position to defend ourselves at any moment.
Certainly no one in any party on this side of the house wants for one moment to weaken the preparation which may be necessary to defend ourselves. But what are we defending ourselves against, and why? We are told, the headlines tell us, we say it here in the house, the Prime Minister has said it, the Minister of Defence Production has said it, we have all said it, that we are defending ourselves in order to maintain our way of life. That is why tonight there are men at the alert on the high seas, in the air and on the land in the armed forces of this country. They are there to maintain our way of life. With all respect to the hon. gentlemen opposite, I say they and we may be paying taxes to defend our way of life but we will vote it away in the House of Commons if we pass legislation such as this. This legislation is contrary to our way of life because it defies and violates the rule of law which we have known, which we have treasured, which we have inherited and which we have defended throughout the centuries. It is unnecessary and it is wrong.


Why maintain armed defences for 35 or 50 years, as the hon. member for Greenwood said, and at the same time bring up a generation, two generations, three generations who will not know at all what the values were which we inherited and which we are intended to preserve? I am not going to speak at length. I feel very strongly about the matter. I believe that we in this country have inherited, as has been the case throughout the commonwealth and the western world generally-certainly in the British commonwealth-a respect and feeling for the rule of law which is not recognized by the bill, which of course is not yet before us but is envisaged by the resolution because we now know what it means. It is going to perpetuate the act on and on and on, one year, five years, 25 years from now. That, sir, is not, as I said, the way of life that I think hon. members of the House of Commons were sent here to preserve and protect.
The hon. member for Greenwood said this is not the horse and buggy age. I can remember when every railroad train in the country was tied up, when transportation was brought to a standstill, and yet we were able to summon parliament within a few days. We came here by car, by plane and perhaps by horse and buggy, but we got here and we dealt with the matter. Is there anyone in the chamber tonight who is going to tell us that we could not deal with a matter of emergency that had to be dealt with quickly and readily if we did not have this legislation?
I trust the minister. I do not think the minister is going to wave a big club or do anything of the kind, but we do not know who is going to succeed him. We do not know what governments may succeed the present government. Obviously and admittedly we must be legislating now for perpetuity, relatively speaking, because, as I said, I do not think there is one of us who does not realize that what we are facing tonight we will continue to face for probably 25 years. That is a figure plucked out of the air. It may be 15 or 50 years. We have to orient our life and conduct accordingly. I have no desire to see us protect ourselves against the communist state and at the same time by legislation at least make it possible to have a fascist state in this country. I do not approve of that, and I oppose it.
I think such legislation is contrary to the rule of law which, as I said, we have inherited and which we cherish. It is certainly ironical to find that it should be introduced by a party which professes to be liberal. It is the very antithesis of liberalism, although that may not be recognized by those who

have been in power for so long that they have forgotten what the word means. I say again that this legislation is unnecessary and wrong. It will have an effect on our children and our children's children.
I do not want to indulge in hyperbole, but this is the opening step of a course, as I see it-I can be wrong, and I hope I am wrong -which we may have to follow for a quarter of a century or half a century; and unless we have the courage, imagination and ability, as I am sure we have and as I am sure the minister has, to legislate slowly, carefully and properly for that period instead of hysterically, erroneously and hastily, then we should not be here at all.
We know that suggestions and urgings perhaps do not have too much effect on a government which feels its responsibility, and a minister who undoubtedly feels that he is proceeding rightly in the course he is following, but I urge the minister again to reconsider this matter and change the legislation in some way so that we can say we are preserving the principles in which we believe, and maintaining the rule of law instead of crucifying it and destroying it. We can face the future, whether it is 5, 10 or 50 years, with confidence under those circumstances, and we cannot do so if we are going to have such legislation as that which confronts us tonight.

Mr. Chairman, I shall not delay the committee long, but I am interested in the legislation from a slightly different point of view than that which has been expressed thus far. May 1 say that I am always interested in hearing the hon. member for Greenwood. I admire his style greatly, and I believe he speaks with more humility than is necessary with respect to his ability.
I sometimes wonder whether he does not give too much credit for omnipotence to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I was so interested in what he had to say tonight that I looked up some Shakespeare and found it very apt in connection with his words. For example, there is the place where Cassius said:
Upon what meat doth this our Caesar feed,
That he Is grown so great?
Perhaps even more apt is the beginning of the passage where he said:
Why, man, he doth bestride the narrow world Like a Colossus; and we petty men Walk under his huge legs, and peep about To find ourselves dishonourable graves.
I am sure that while the minister was speaking there was another thought running 50433-125

Whatever the situation may be, whether the powers the government is requesting are too great with respect to what has to be done, I shall not enter into that argument at this late hour. But there is one feature about this act in which I am interested from the taxpayers' point of view, and upon which I would ask the minister to throw a little light. I refer to the power that is contained in, I believe, section 16 of the act, which sets up a revolving fund of some $100 million for the minister to use as he sees fit for the purpose of making advances, loans and investments in plant, equipment and supplies.
I realize that a rather substantial portion of that money has been used for crown companies of various kinds. There has been a substantial amount also used to provide what is called capital assistance to private industry. I believe that since the powers granted under the act make it possible for the minister to use these funds without the authority of the governor in council and certainly without any further authority from parliament, the taxpayer should know upon what basis and under what circumstances this capital assistance, loans and advances are granted.
I find, for example, that some fairly well established industries have received rather substantial amounts. The minister has emphasized that he has had no difficulty in placing defence contracts with the various industries. I am not surprised, because it would appear to me to be a very lucrative type of business. Presumably the manufacturers obtain the contract at a profit, so I do not know why the minister would expect anything different. In addition the industries are provided with capital assistance and accelerated depreciation which, in effect, means that the government is financing the production of the goods under a contract at a profit to the industrialist.
I should like to know under what circumstances such assistance is provided; whether it is on the basis of the need of the industry; whether it is on the basis of the importance of the particular contract to be granted, or whether it is on the basis of a lack of the proper kind of plant and equipment necessary to complete the contract. I should like to know also on what basis this money is repayable, and whether there is any interest on these advances or investments in private

Defence Production Act industry. It is necessary to know all these things, because the amounts that have been used under the authority of this act are rather substantial. As I said, some of that money has gone to crown companies, and of course that is a different matter.
I find on looking through the Public Accounts that such firms, for example, as Canadian General Electric have been advanced an amount of $2,868,187 over the whole period, $218,533 of which has been within the last fiscal year. Canadian Pratt and Whitney Aircraft Company has been provided with $6,635,354, of which $564,028 was within the last fiscal year. The John Inglis Company of Toronto, a rather well known company in relation to defence contracts, has been given $6,852,396, of which $1,302,622 was within the last year. We go on down the line and come to A. V. Roe Limited of Malton, and they have been provided with $54,764,225, of which $7,174,679 was within the last fiscal year.
These are large amounts, and although I would not at this time cast any doubts or suspicions about the way in which this money is handled, when the taxpayers, whose money it is after all, see the way that money can be used without reference to parliament, without even reference to the governor in council, then the taxpayers want to know on what basis such advances are made.
What is the basis of repayment? Is there any interest payable on such advances? What are the circumstances under which the decision is made? I hope the minister will throw some light on that particular part of the act before this resolution passes.

We were taken a bit by surprise, Mr. Chairman, at the change in the program. We had expected there would be a report from the Minister of National Defence and then a discussion concerning fisheries, but suddenly we were plunged into this matter which many members of the house feel is of grave importance.
That is because of the special powers.

I was impressed by the presentation made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra tonight in setting out so clearly the wide powers that are contained in the bill, and drawing the attention of the house to the seriousness of the situation. He was, of course, followed by other members on this side. Yesterday the hon. member for Eglinton drew attention to the seriousness of this measure. It so happens that tonight we find ourselves discussing it a bit on the spur of the moment, but that does not take anything away from its importance.
[Mr. Zaplitny.l

I notice that when the Prime Minister was dealing with this subject yesterday he anticipated that there might be some objection to continuing the powers contained in this bill. On page 1905 of Hansard for March 10, 1955, he said:
I would point out that many of these powers are required to complete the present program-the aircraft portion of that program now extends at least into 1960-and to carry out the continuing functions of the department.
There are other powers which are not being used at this time but which were placed there because they were considered to be essential in dealing with any emergency which might arise-
That was not a full explanation of the need for continuing these powers. In the course of the Prime Minister's remarks, and in the course of the remarks of the Minister of Defence Production tonight, the cloak of respectability has been placed over this department. As I see it, there is no objection advanced here with regard to the necessity for the Department of Defence Production. It has proven to be necessary in these times. We are not raising any objection at this moment with regard to the administration of that department. We have respect for the minister in charge at the moment, and consequently have nothing critical to say now concerning him or his department.
We consider that department is essential. As has been pointed out, it was given these powers at a time of critical emergency, when the Korean war was at its height, and when no one was sure as to whether or not that war might develop into something larger. Although objections were made to the powers contained in the act, it was passed.
But that was a period of intense, critical emergency. The suggestion is now made to us that there is a continuing crisis. We recognize the fact; there is a continuing crisis. We do not know where at any moment some war may break out. We cannot guess as to its magnitude. But since the conclusion of the Korean war we have not been quite as hard-pressed along that line.
However, I find in the Prime Minister's statement something which would indicate a sense of urgency at the moment, and perhaps we should have more information as to what that urgency is. Perhaps we should be prepared in our minds for some additional trouble in the world. If there is a tremendous sense of urgency at the moment, why should we be left in doubt? If there is such a sense of urgency with regard to the Department of Defence Production, then I submit that sense of urgency should be shown by other departments of government.
Where is the sense of urgency in respect to civil defence? I have not seen anything that

has inclined me to the belief that the minister in charge of that department is at all alarmed. What city is prepared for evacuation? What plans have been made to preserve important documents here in Ottawa? There does not seem to be any sense of urgency there. And what is the sense of urgency in the Department of National Defence? I have been wondering about that for several years. There are many things I think should be done by that department, if we are facing an immediate crisis. Has our airborne brigade ever been exercised as an airborne brigade? Where do we stand on the question of armour, which I have discussed in the house on other occasions? Where are our forces? I do not think there is any sense of urgency displayed on the part of the Department of National Defence.
Tonight the minister put clearly the case for the Department of Defence Production, and I agreed with his presentation. There is a sense of urgency with regard to critical materials. We are prepared to admit that, and to say that certain powers may be necessary in regard to preparations concerning aircraft, electronics, munitions and the like, as has been mentioned already by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and others. If the minister needs to make preparations along those lines we are not going to say him nay. But we do not see the need for what we consider to be excessive powers.
Here we have an act which was going to run out this year, and certainly its life was to be for five years. At the time of the Korean crisis people were prepared to accept something of that nature, but we are hardly prepared to accept it indefinitely. Surely we will not live under the tension of a crisis all our lives. Or, if it is going to come to a head very shortly, then parliament must be taken into the confidence of the government and told what powers are required. Because the strength of our parliamentary system of democracy is simply this, that in a time of emergency we surrender our powers, powers inherent in the House of Commons, and place them in the hands of the prime minister or the cabinet and tell them to get on with the job. When the crisis has subsided those powers are relinquished.

That has been the history of parliamentary democracy as practised by British peoples. That has been the history of parliamentary democracy as practised here in Canada, and I think we should continue along that line. Give powers in times of crisis, and let those powers be relinquished when the crisis has subsided. At the moment the crisis of the Korean war has subsided, and so far as we know we are not now under the same urgency as we were then. Consequently, as has been said several times tonight, we are agreeing to the setting up of this department on a permanent basis, but not with the absolute and all-inclusive powers now contained in the act.
